en: Hari bows to that pair of claws, which were truly realized upon the sight of the enraged Hiraṇyakaśipu, and which were as deep-set as the broad chest-plate of the golden-hued [demon]. (Līlā 1) Bow to Him, who at that time, while lifting up the three worlds with His third step, made them appear like a mere trifle. (Līlā 1)

Līlā 2: Bow again with silence to that very foot of his, which was seated upon the threshold itself while he was being laughed at by the plowman, as it remained fixed there while crossing the threshold with a body that had not yet reached its full size.

Līlā 3: Bow again with silence to that very foot of his, which was seated upon the threshold itself while he was being laughed at by the plowman, as it remained fixed there while crossing the threshold with a body that had not yet reached its full size.

May he be victorious, whose arm-jewel— dark as a rain-cloud, increasing the onset of the calamitous monsoon, and which served as the executioner for the demon Rīṭṭha— fell upon the neck of that demon.
(Līlā 4) May the jewel-lamps on the hoods of Śeṣa, resting upon the couch of the great serpent, protect you.
Victory to Hari, who is like a sprout from the bulbous root of the moon’s navel, which has burst forth;
who utters his roar as the remaining serpents, crushed by the fire of the churning of the ocean, let out their shrieks;
and who has awakened from his sleep upon the water-dwellers stirred by the wind. (Līlā 5A)
Bow to Hari’s two arms, which possess the power to break, crush, toss about, pull out, and support the Yamala, Arjuna, Riṣṭa, Keśin, Kaṃsa, the Lord of Asuras, and the mountains. (Līlā.
6) His face filled with his rough forearms, he is possessed by the strength of his hard hands.
Victory to the slayer of Madhu, who is difficult to behold even for the gods with their eyes fixed upon the tips of their hair!

(Līlā 7) Victory to him by whom the seven oceans were swallowed like a single mouthful, as if they were mere drops, within his mouth which was filled with the intent to devour the three worlds! (Līlā 8)

Bow to the foot of Gaurī, which bears the smooth anklets from the heads of the prostrating gods and demons, and which was raised by the breaking of the skull of the buffalo burdened by its heavy load.
(Līlā 9) [The foot] moistened by the perspiration from the exertion of pulling out Caṇḍī’s hard, round head...

May the bodice of the daughter of the Sun, overflowing with saffron flowers, protect you always. (Līlā 10) May the surging waves of the celestial river, mingled with the rays of the moon and white with the flashing, loud laughter [of Śiva], destroy your sin. (Līlā 11)

Those sun-like virtuous people are truly selfless, for whom even the accumulation of gold blossoms upon meeting with those who possess faults, as if bound by a single thread, like a cluster of lotuses.
May he be victorious, by whom even the good have been fashioned here in this world as if they were wicked. (Līlā. 12)
Even the rays of the moon do not suffer diminution without that [moon].
(Līlā 13) Homage always to both the wicked and the virtuous whose minds are intent on the affairs of others:
some are by nature scurrilous, while others are averse to the faults of others. (Līlā 14)
Alternatively, no fault whatsoever is seen in the entire world of living beings; everyone indeed possesses good eyes.
Listen to what we shall say:
even through association with the virtuous, the impurity of the wicked does not depart. (Līlā 15)
Even though situated in the middle of the moon’s orb, the deer remains black.
(Līlā 16) Even through association with the wicked, the virtue of a good person does not perish;
likewise, although her mouth is salty, her lower lip still exudes honey. (Līlā 16A)
Enough with this pursuit of irrelevant conversation, which is like the idle sport of fools— a mere attachment to meaningless talk.
(Līlā 17) There was once [a time] when the gods were filled with joy by the contact with the fires of the triple oblation.
He who has attained the fruit of the fivefold assembly and is known by the name Bahulārcis— Līlā 18.
Even today, the moon bears his chest, as if soiled by crests of smoke spreading from its great fire, under the guise of its deer-mark— Līlā 19.
To him, that great ocean of the jewels of virtue, was born a single son named Bhūṣaṇabhaṭṭa, who was like the moon in the sky of his own lineage. (Līlā.
20) By whose Vedas, emerging from the four mouths as if they were dear kinsmen—

"My own self was highly esteemed by those who rested upon the single lotus of his mouth. (Līlā.21) "Listen, therefore, to this jewel of a narrative named *Līlāvatī*, composed out of curiosity by one such as me, though lacking in substance. (Līlā.22)

Just as on an autumn night, when the frontal globes of the elephant of darkness have been split by the moon’s rays—serving as the lion’s claws—and which is radiant with scattered pearls from the sky, [she spoke].
At the hour of twilight, seated comfortably upon a couch in the upper chamber of her white palace, she said: "Dear one, look, look! (Līlā 23)

In the house canal, white with the luster of the moonlight flooding its banks and fragrant with scented pastes applied to every limb, the six-legged bee—drinking the delicious, thick nectar of the *tiṅgicchī* flowers while humming sweetly—wanders without hindrance as the petals of the blossoming *candujjuā* unfold. (Līlā 24) By this autumn, the moon [shines]; by the moon, the night; and by the night, the lotus grove.
The flock of swans shines like a sandy bank with a bed of white water-lilies, and the sandy bank like the flock of swans with the white water-lilies. (Līlā.25) O listen!
The melodious warbling of the swans, beautiful with throats purified by fresh sprouts of *viśaka*, resembles the tinkling of anklets on the feet of the River Sarasvatī. (Līlā.26)
The breeze blows, cooled by contact with the waves of the cool, flowing water, and heavy with the fragrance of the slightly blossomed buds of the *mālatī* jasmine;
this [lake] too, in its fresh waters, is like a row of various faces belonging to the ten directions. (Līlā 27)
The forest grove, with its trees whose branches sway in the shimmering ripples, seems to endure [the heat].
(Līlā 28) Behold, in the ponds, these cakravāka birds—whose hearts are fixed solely on the imagination of day—are now free from the pain of separation. (Līlā 29)
Thus the swarm of bees wanders about, drawn by the delight of the fragrance of the blossoming *saptaparna* flowers, never abandoning their longing for the clusters of blossoms.
(Līlā 30) [The night] possesses the splendor of moonlight and the moisture of fragrant *kuvalaya* lilies in full bloom.
The moon, as it were, drinks the face of the night, which possesses a sky of stainless stars.
(Līlā 31) So, what is the use of much speaking?
The night is most delightful, the autumn is pure, and you yourself are at hand.
In the company of those who are well-disposed toward me, I believe there is nothing that does not exist.
Therefore, O Līlā, tell us some extraordinary, sweet story—delightful merely by its evening recitation, charming in its discourse, and pleasing to the hearts of women. (Līlā 32–33)

Having heard those words from the lotus-like mouths of his head, O lady with eyes like blue water-lilies, the poets have declared that there are three kinds of narratives here: the divine (*divyā*), the semi-divine (*divyamānuṣī*), and the human (*mānuṣī*). (Līlā.
34) Just as the divine is [described], so is the semi-divine; and just as the semi-divine, so too is the human.
Even there, it is said that some early poets composed certain characteristics [of poetry]. (Līlā.
35) Furthermore, various excellent stories (*sukathā*) composed in the *Suvarṇaraitaka* style—which is free from the faults of *śakārapāda*—are heard from the preeminent great poets. (Līlā. 36)
Among them, those stories which are taught by ignorant people like us do not find favor in the world, O fair-eyed one. (Līlā.
37) Therefore, O gentle lady, why do you mock me with your unlearned knowledge of grammar?
Even to utter it is not possible, much less to compose a vast narrative.
And it was said by my beloved: "O dear one, what is the use of that science of grammar, by which the path of pleasant speech has been blocked for people like us? (Līlā 38–39)

"That very sound which is eternal and by which the meaning is clearly perceived through a heart that has not been rendered useless—that alone is our primary characteristic; what need have we for other definitions? (Līlā 40).
Thus she spoke in a language charming to the hearts of simple young women.
"Tell me, tell me that divine-human story, which possesses auspicious marks in rare regions.
(Līlā 41) Having heard that, she spoke again: "O you with eyes like the face of a young deer, if it is so, then let the subject matter of the story be heard, well-composed in its joints. (Līlā 42)
And there is [the goddess] who possesses the beauty of a vast upward-arched brow bound by a girdle of the four oceans,
and who supports the earth with all her limbs resting upon the moon-like head of Śeṣa. (Līlā 43)
To the venerable Earth, who is adorned with various jewels and possesses a weightiness born from the attainment of the joy of uplifting the world from the boar-incarnation, [Līlā 44:
the multitude of all the common folk is delighted by the attainment of every kind of crop.
The interior of which is filled with the sounds of the bellowing of bulls from the villages of Suvvasia;
where the gardens are agitated by the cries of the courtesans at the very pleasant market-stalls for grain;
it is renowned as the abode of all happiness and the object of longing. (Līlā 45–46)
The Yogaśāstra is inseparable from the Dharma that accomplishes all aims;
it is like the foundation of the sciences, a dwelling place for the virtuous, a teaching for merits, and the very birthplace of multitudes of happiness. (Līlā 47)
The noble man is like a well-irrigated field for his virtues. (Līlā 48) Furthermore: A cowherd community is delighted by its herd of cattle, which are content with very succulent fodder.
The quarters were filled with joy amidst the multitude of the excellent Vallaī and Veṇu flutes. (Līlā 49)

It was a reservoir of pure water, easy to enter; delightful with the splendor of lush groves of trees; its surface adorned by clusters of lotus ponds; crowded with travelers seeking shelter beneath the branches of fruit-bearing trees bent low with their heavy loads; free from all calamities; endowed with the four castes; ever-increasing in joy through perpetual festivals; its ground beautified by various forests; its interior spaces perfumed by the fragrance of diverse flowers; untouched by the Kali age; devoid of sin; never abandoning righteousness; where vice was unperceived; its beauty undiminished; free from the fear of thieves and kings; and a dwelling place for an immeasurable multitude of virtues.
And where the blessed Pajjanna rains down desires; where the wish-fulfilling trees are fragrant, the forest creepers bear fruit, and young women are never barren.
And where the women have breasts heavy with thick sandalwood paste and arms as tender as lotus stalks.
The women with sweet voices are like rivers. (Līlā 50) Let alone its own fields;
even the rest [of the land] is guarded by the wives of the common folk, who have driven away the deer with the charming sounds of their songs. (Līlā 51)
O beautiful one, in the midst of such a circle of virtuous friends, there is a delightful city named Païṭṭhāṇa,
which is the abode of all happiness. (Līlā 52) And while that dear city is being described, the night passes away.
I shall speak something to you by way of a brief summary; listen.
(Līlā 53) There, the royal swans, following the sound of the anklets on the feet of beautiful women, cause their beaks—filled with fresh lotus shoots—to resound in echo. (Līlā 54)
The domestic peacocks dance upon the moonstone slabs, their eyes fixed with singular delight upon the sky made dark by the smoke from the sacrificial fires.
(Līlā 55) It is impossible to move within [the house], where the mass of darkness is obstructed by the network of rays from the household jewels.
Even though they have cast off their ornaments, they wander about with their gait unimpeded;
in this city where the mass of sunbeams is incessantly pierced by the rays of jewels set in golden pillars, the courtesans proceed to the assembly hall for the concert. (Līlā 56–57)

Where the groves of *kalakaṇṭhī* birds, intoxicated by the passion of amorous women whose pride has been shattered by the boar of Spring, make even the beloveds feel as if they were in a second spring;
where the spray from the drops of perspiration of amorous women, exhausted by the urgency of their haste, [refreshes them]. (Līlā 58)
Where the garden breezes are drunk in by hands folded in salutation;
where the swans, longing for lotus stalks, desire the moonlight reflected from the cheeks of amorous women sleeping on the roofs of their houses. (Līlā 59–60)
In the Godāvarī river, where the waters are stained tawny by the turmeric from the breasts of the Marahatthī women, the sins of that very day are washed away. (Līlā.
61) However, there is one drawback: the scent of the mallikā jasmine at the onset of summer.

It does not even allow the amorous gestures of proud women to be enjoyed, for they are pleasant only in private. However, there is one drawback: the amorous play of young women on that crystal surface is visible even to people standing outside. (Līlā 62 & 62A)

But there is one drawback there: the painted walls of the houses are obscured by the mass of pollen from blossoming flowers, driven by the force of the wind. (Līlā 63) In such a city as that, [he] whose body was embraced by every excellence...
King Śālavāhana by name, whose fame has spread throughout the world.
(Līlā 64) He, though bodiless, is yet beautiful with all his limbs;
though difficult for people to behold, he is the producer of joy for their eyes. (Līlā 65)

Even though he is a merchant, he is beloved by his clients; likewise, even though he is a newcomer, he is courageous; and even though he fears the next world, he is truly single-mindedly devoted to heroism. (Līlā.
66) Even though he is a sun, he is not hot; even though he is the moon, he is forever free from blemish.
Though he is humble, he is not double-tongued; though he is lofty, he bestows fruit upon those nearby.

(Līlā 67) Like the moon on days of the waning fortnight, by him the entire circle of his enemies has been reduced to a mere semblance of a disc, marked by the suffering of their own emaciation. (Līlā 68)
Like the moon whose orb is subdued by its own setting, he whose back was never seen by another in battle when he had been overtaken by his enemies— Līlā 69.
He passed his nights in mountain caves, reddened by the contact with the tips of medicinal herbs.
By the power of whose majesty, as if his enemies were already subdued,
beautiful women— whose hands are reddened by the rays of their jeweled nails— paint him upon the walls of their own dwellings under the guise of the God of Love. (Līlā 70–71)

Even those poetic compositions which have been long contemplated by wise poets wither away within their hearts without him, like the desires of the unfortunate; such was the case for that great lord of the earth, whose wealth was boundless according to his will.
(Līlā 72) Thus, of that sovereign of the great earth, whose prosperity exceeded his desires...
O gentle one, the month of Madhumāsa has arrived like a messenger from the god whose arrows are flowers.
(Līlā 73) The forests seem to announce the departure of Spring, first heralded by the fragrant breeze, now by the abundant, warbling cries of the cuckoos. (Līlā 74)
Holding a mango blossom in his beak, the parrot wanders with leaves in his claws;
O King of the Frost, depart! For the Earth has been won by Spring. (Līlā.
74) Amidst the closing buds and the masses of blossoming flowers...
Lakṣmī places her foot upon the forests in exactly the same way as she does upon springtime. (Līlā 75) What is the use of many increasing arrows for the flower-bowed god?
He needs only a single mango sprout; it is not enough [for him]. (Līlā 76)
In spring, the forest of *kaṇiār* trees, its beauty enhanced by the splendor of the blooming tilaka flowers, surpasses even golden ornaments in its loveliness. (Līlā.
77) The great trees are completely enveloped by the glory of the various blossoms of the forest deities in full bloom.

How much more so, then, does the blooming *mallikā* not do? (Līlā 78) The *pāṭala* flower first makes the hearts of the lover tender; afterwards, the remaining arrows of the flower-god enter them with ease. (Līlā 79)
The groves of *māndava* trees, with their masses of thick foliage and broad leaves that are heavy with full-blown flowers, become difficult for travelers to look upon. (Līlā.
80) [The groves] where the dense mass of petals is obscured by bees flying up from the abundant flowers...
In Kundalāikā, the flower that had been parched by the heat of separation from frost is now blooming.
(Līlā 81) Even though gently shaken by a slight breeze, the sinduvāra flowers have shed their blossoms, their joints and bonds loosened by the sap oozing from the wounds of being struck. (Līlā 82)
When spring had been discerned by the lotus, whose face was covered in the mud of intense heat,
she laughed, as it were, having recovered from the burden of the cold that had passed away.
(Līlā 83) [She] is on all sides [adorned] with rays of light cast forth through the joy of encountering the Malaya breeze.
The beauty of spring is carried forth by branches as dark as fresh sprouts.
(Līlā 84) In the avenues of the *palāśa* groves, with their masses of blossoming flowers, the month of Madhu appears like a newly married bridegroom, his body draped in red garments. (Līlā 85)
The joyful month of Madhu (Spring) increases in the mango groves, enters the bowers of fresh mādhavī vines, and seems to dally with the rows of *kaṅkelli* leaves;
it is touched by the breeze carrying the fragrance gathered from various forest creepers. (Līlā 86)

The young mango tree seems to weep with its flower-fingers as it turns its face away. (Līlā 87) Lovers are overwhelmed by Kāma, who has found his opportunity and dwells within the entire expanse of their blooming eyes, piercing them with his flower-arrows. (Līlā 88)

When the entire world of living beings had been brought under the sway of the arrows of the god of love, the King arrived at the pavilion that served as the site for his union with the Goddess of Spring. Līlā. 89.
[The ground] was strewn with the rays from the rubies in the crowns of the vassal lords who had come to pay their respects.

Seated upon his lion-throne amidst the sound of the bards' songs of victory, he was surrounded by courtesans like a lord of the gods by celestial nymphs; or like the city of Kanakāvalī with its horses, he sat with his wives whose faces were ever smiling. (Līlā 90–91)
Then that lord of men conversed with Candalekhā, who was alone with him, in a manner that was playful, most charming, and pleasant:
“O Candalekhā, do you not notice the rain of flower-pollen driven by the Malaya breeze? (Līlā. 92)
By Love, the ten directions have been fashioned like a pleasure-palace.
O moon-faced one, why then have you been completely overwhelmed today by some kinsman of the arrows of Māra with such total exertion across your entire body? (Līlā 93–94)
By whom was this bee, as if alive, painted upon the surface of your forehead— its face nestled within a fresh campaka flower,
and it intoxicated by the drinking of honey?
(Līlā 95) Or rather, by what highly precious collyrium of the serpent of Love has it been applied to your cheeks?
The lines drawn on the leaf are like the arrows of Love.
(Līlā 96) O gentle one, by whom and when was this mango blossom, its cluster of flowers shaken by the touch of a hand, fashioned upon the edge of your cheek? (Līlā 97)
By whom today, as he draws the bowstring, has the glory of the leaf been attained upon the slope of your breasts, which are yellow like a mass of refined gold?
(Līlā 98) Each word is like a lotus stalk, its neck bent low in the act of drawing.
"By whom was this pair of swans drawn upon the lotus-feet?
(Līlā 99) Thus, by whom—with a heart moved by the desire to manifest his own learning, yet incapable of distinguishing between merit and fault—was the milk of the *sappiṇī* era drunk? (Līlā 100)
Having heard that, Candalekhā, her face with its eyes wide open at the sight of the king,
spoke with words of slight shame and bashfulness: "O King, that Citrāṅgada is skilled in piercing [targets], by whom— [at] your door— " *Līlā* 101.
Having taken up the leaf, you yourself were then painted [there].
(Līlā 102) That very same person has now come here from the island of Siṃhala;
by him, everything has been fully depicted during this festival of love. (Līlā 103)
While the king was thus established in the pleasure of a humorous assembly, one minister, having found an opportunity, spoke:
"O Lord, I believe that spy was dispatched by the King of Siṃhala. (Līlā. 104)
By virtue of this wisdom, she dwells in the house of Candralekhā.
(Līlā 105) Those such as these who remain in the retinues of kings are called "Yakṣas" by people in this world;
they are the spies. (Līlā 106)
The king said: "O gentle lady, Vijayānanda was sent against him by the Lord of Siṃhala, accompanied by the minister Poṭṭisa-vara.
Even today, no one from his camp has returned to tell the truth. (Līlā 106A)
"What does the Lord of Siṃhala say, or what does our commander-in-chief say? Līlā:
"This very day, messengers have reported that Vijayānanda, whose power has increased along with Pōṭṭiṣeṇa, has arrived at the shore of the ocean."
Likewise, that King of Siṃhala, tireless on that very day, himself fearlessly prepared difficult passes filled with fuel for the horses;
he made the coastal shores uneven and joined together the battlefields. (Līlāvatī 108)
"Accompanied by Vijayānanda, the great battle proceeds undaunted.
(Līlā 109) And the King said: "Dear kinsman, Vijayānanda himself has arrived there and is established in his own office of peace and war; what need have we for this man? (Līlā 110)
How could Vijayānanda be deceived by the Lord of Siṃhala—he who has terrified even other great mandala-lords, though they were fearless? (Līlā.
111) Report this constantly to your messenger, exactly as it was told to you.
"Let this delightful pleasure-pavilion pass by for now," having spoken thus,
the king bestowed great festival-attainments upon all the courtesans and many gifts upon the bards. (Līlā 112–113)

Having thus been honored, with his face radiant with the joy of delighting all his subjects, the Lord was approached and addressed by the family priest: "O King, it is nearly midday; even the bath itself causes me weariness. (Līlā 114)
His mind was constantly fixed on entering your door, for he was devoted to you alone.
Then, having dismissed all his attendants and commenced his bath, he set forth amidst the clamor of "Victory!
raised by a multitude of bards.

Meanwhile, a tumultuous commotion arose in the assembly hall, mingled with the clamor of warriors and mixed with the cries of the most excellent ladies of the great king’s harem who were being jostled;
it was a scene where faces were crushed and tossed about by the violent trampling of men suddenly rising up. (Līlā.
117) He fell down, his face smeared by the impact of the crushing and tossing of men who rose up all at once.
The venerable Bhaṭṭa cried out, "Alas! I am ruined, I am utterly ruined! (Līlā 118).
Then that wretched man, having been ensnared by the trap of service, was somehow or other dragged out by the king's men like an old elephant stuck in the mud. (Līlā 119)
In the meantime,
the people stationed at each courtyard pillar remember one another with pleasure as the clusters of rubies fallen from their crowns rubbing against each other slip away. (Līlā 120)
Some excellent courtesans, though themselves prostitutes, stand in front and are pushed aside by the broad breasts of those most beloved to their lovers. (Līlā.
121) Some [women], their movement obstructed by the mass of sweat from the great crush, [proceed slowly].

Even though her girdle has been cast off, the weight of her hips has become difficult to abandon. (Līlā 122) To a woman longing for an embrace with one who is desired by her heart, even a broken necklace of large, pure pearls is highly esteemed when he has arrived. (Līlā 123)

"Even though the region has been found by me, it is somehow passed with difficulty after a long time— by her whose eyes are closed like lotuses as they meet the fragrance of my mouth. (Līlā 1.124) Thus,
having sent away his attendants with this signal, he somehow departed from the royal palace.
With his heart breathing a sigh of relief, the world returned to its own abode.
And the king [departed] amidst various musical instruments resounding with auspicious hymns,
and with throngs of bards and panegyrists chanting.
Having bathed for a long time with all the medicinal herbs indeed,
and having performed the propitiatory rites for the gods and others as prescribed by the entire assembly, he returned to his palace.
(Līlā 127) There too, having given gifts consisting of land, cows, gold, garments, and sesame seeds...
Having entered the dining hall of the bestowers of gifts,
with a gracious disposition, he ate various delicious foods appropriate for the occasion together with the friends of that region who were his devotees. (Līlā 128–129)
Surrounded by his retinue who had gathered at that time, he entered the inner assembly hall where an excellent jeweled couch had been prepared;
seated there with his companions, who followed the styles of the good poets, [he enjoyed himself]. (Līlā 130)
The king, entirely happy and contented, was addressed by the gatekeeper at the Single River—
who was skilled in discerning the state of his master’s heart— with a staff held in his left hand and a fly-whisk in his right. (Līlā 131–132)
"Your Majesty, the commander-in-chief Vijayānanda, the attendant of Jarākapphaṇa, stands at the gate for some purpose. (Līlā 133) Then,
hearing that suddenly, with a mind filled with sorrow and wonder—
The Lord of the Earth, his eyes fixed upon the face of the minister, said:
“O venerable Kumārila, you have heard what Vaitālika has related;
has Vijayānanda then fallen into such a state? (Līlā 134–135)
"Even though his intellect is expanded by a vast knowledge of the principles of all the sciences without exception,
how has he come here alone, without a vehicle?
(Līlā 136) There are no servants here, nor elephants, nor horses, nor even a footman or a minister."
"How has Vijayānanda come to such a state?
The noble prince replied: "O King, I consider the course of events in this world to be unpredictable;
nevertheless, he has arrived here for some purpose."
Why is this?
For men whose great majesty has increased and who have not completed their mission in such a momentous task, death alone is endured. (Līlā. 138)
Therefore, if even this King of Siṃhala has met with defeat, he will surely not enter your gate alive; for what is the use of deliberation regarding the course of one's own destiny? (Līlā.
139) Indeed, that very same fate awaits him.
"Bring him here; do not delay! Let his facial expression be seen!
(Līlā 140) Then, following the path of the gatekeepers who had been instantly commanded by the king, he was brought before the lord of men, his lotus-like head crushed by the jaws of a dog.
(Līlā 141)
Having been honored by the Lord, O beautiful one, a comfortable seat was commanded for him;
he sat down, his eyes fixed upon the feet of Bhaṭṭakumāril. Then, having occupied that comfortable seat there and having made the place secluded— Līlā 142.
a. Now, having taken possession of that comfortable seat and having rendered it solitary...
Having been consoled for a moment, he was asked by the Lord about his welfare. Līlā 143:
"O Vijayānanda, this meeting of yours here, devoid of all propriety, grieves my heart exceedingly. Līlā 144.
Having heard these words of his master, which were followed by such compassion, he, with eyes wide open from the weight of joy, replied:
"O Lord, this is indeed a great story; it is the fulfillment of our most cherished desires. (Līlā 1.145)

Out of curiosity, listen with attentive hearts. (Līlā 1.46) When the Lord of the Malaya region had been brought under control, and when Paṇḍirāja had begun the undertaking of crossing over to the opposite shore of the ocean of jewels.
(Līlā 1.47)
The minister Śrī-Poṭṭiṣeṇa said: "Do not act so rashly;
the rain-cloud is not something for us to subdue with force.
Even an ordinary man in a difficult situation cannot be overcome by the enemy's soldiers. (Līlā. 148)
He, moreover, was complete in his faculties, brave, generous, and a loyal friend.
(Līlā 149) Possessed of sound reasoning, patient, and unassailable by his superiors, he was highly honorable;
yet, though preeminent in counsel and majesty, he was pained when provoked by enemies. (Līlā 150)
"Vigilance should be maintained by all kings; for although this earth belongs to everyone, men do not become possessors of fortune through the mere relish of their own prowess alone.
(Līlā 151) Therefore, while conciliation exists, and while there is a discernment of the differences among men..."

Therefore, let a messenger be dispatched—one who stands firm on the edge of a sword-blade, skilled in discerning the inner feelings of others, clever, knowing the right time, and resolute.
(Līlā 154) If he returns with that very [result], then tell me; what is the use of further display?

What is the use of giving poison to one who has already perished by it? (Līlā 155) And I have heard that he has a beloved daughter named Līlāvatī, born from the very essence of the entire world of living beings, dearer to him than his own life. (Līlā 156)

That lord of the entire earth shall attain divine perfections. (Līlā 158) Therefore, if somehow he were to present that jewel of a maiden to our master, then what would not be accomplished for us on this earth? (Līlā 159)

Though its marrow has decayed and it is now sapless, it remains indeed full of flavor;

The slopes of the shore appear like the floral offerings made by the goddess Śrī upon the mountain of her abode,

The departure of Varuṇī is indicated by its filaments;

In that place, where the breeze is perfumed by the fragrance of cloves and cardamom, and which is frequented by pairs of perfected beings (*siddhas*) in their golden swan-like palaces,
the footstool of the tree [of Indra] is worn smooth by the friction of the crowns of the heads of gods and demons. (Līlā 175)
Having bowed to Rāmeśvara, he boarded a boat. (Līlā 176) Though lacking noble lineage, it is well-versed in the scriptures; though devoid of feet, it possesses a swift gait;
though composed of many qualities, it is light; and though without water, it holds many passengers. (Līlā 177)
O King, while that boat, with its limited crew, had not yet crossed the ocean, he ascended a single river [of tears]. (Līlā.
178) Uprooting the forests of trees on the shore and filling the mouths of the directions—

There too, with the joints and bonds crushed by the uneven rocky slopes,

"O Līlā, 185. As many calamities as there are born of unrighteousness in this worldly existence—therefore go!
For the body and wealth, all their splendor can be obtained again and again;
just as the moon, though waned, attains that very same long-lasting prosperity once more. 186.
O Lord of Men, having thus heard these words, as unbearable as a thunderbolt’s fall, I somehow or other turned my self away from the jaws of death.
(Līlā 187) For I did not consider your companions, nor did I deliberate upon the task at hand.

There is no personal gain for me, nor honor from my master, nor fame. (Līlā 188) The grief caused by the destruction of my excellent retinue does not so much pain my heart as does this undertaking of mine, which has failed to achieve the purpose desired by my heart. (Līlā 189)

Those men who are capable of receiving commissions, who undertake tasks without indolence, who carry out their duties alone, and who bear a burden as if it were measured out—they are truly some other kind of persons altogether. (Līlā.
190) How could there be such [men] as we, who are destitute of human effort, intelligence, and divine fortune?
"Even such great undertakings as these succeed for lords of the earth.

Even from those who have left wretched villages, instruction is received during times of adversity; for whom among those sinking down do even blades of grass provide a hand to grasp? (Līlā.
193) Therefore, having gone back to Sakkaḍaa with other companions...
"I have prepared myself with the desire to bring the work half-finished to its completion.

Having traversed a forest thicket on the shore of the ocean, where the trees are permeated with the fragrance of cardamom, sandalwood, nutmeg,

O Lord, how indeed, after a long time, did that formidable region of the seven Godāvarīs—filled with groves of *puṇṇāga*, *nāga-kesara*, *jambū*, *kāmra*, and *amba* trees;
its waters divided into seven mouths; and its mud-stained impurities washed away by the flow of those streams—become accessible? (Līlā 197–198)
In the Golā river, whose waters are as vast as the ocean, my fatigue vanished;
even in great calamities, those who have come together through living in the same place are dear. (Līlā 199) Having abandoned all exertion by bathing at will, that very palace of Piṇākin [Śiva]—

Having approached Him who removes the state of worldly existence, he was immediately beheld by Bhavabhūti as one whose feet are touched by the crowns fallen from the heads of all the lords of gods and demons, who is the destroyer of the pride of the three cities, the enemy of Kama, and the husband of the Daughter of the Mountain. (Līlā 200–201)
Having offered praise with devotion through hymns from the science of yoga to the Wielder of the Trident—

sitting on one side in a place comfortably situated for solitude. *Līlāvatī* 2.202.
Like a beautiful and excellent palace in the next world, charming to behold—
there, the arrangement of her neck, with its string of white jasmine flowers hanging down in modesty, surpassed the splendor of the moon by the transformation of her graceful bearing. (Līlā 203–204)
Adorned with a white sacred thread, wearing a rosary as his only ornament, seated upon a simple wooden stool, and without any possessions,
he was seen dressed like a naked ascetic. Then,
after I had offered my salutations, he directed me to take a seat of cane.
Then, having been offered a comfortable seat, he was asked about his welfare. Līlā said:
"From where have you come? Where was your journey intended?
And I replied, "Venerable sir, it was in connection with a pilgrimage to a sacred ford. Līlā.206–207.
Thus, many conversations concerning the meaning of the scriptures arose between us;
like one long acquainted, he has entered into a state of affection toward me. (Līlā 208) Just then, O King, while the Lord of the Day was stationed in the midst of the vault of the sky...
I was addressed thus by that great maharṣi regarding the ocean:
"O one of great intelligence, here we are practitioners of difficult penance who subsist on fruits and roots;
however, food suitable for you cannot be obtained here by any means. (Līlā 209–210)
"Nevertheless, wait for just a moment until I have wandered about and brought back some food that we may enjoy as it is our own.

In this matter, O King, my own experience has become a source of great wonder, as if it were a truth revealed by a seer: because of your absence, the forest has filled its alms-bowl itself with various fruits;
for you, nothing at all is difficult to obtain. (Līlā 212–213)

Then, O King, once my task was accomplished, I was made by him to eat those succulent fruits of the trees there with all hospitality. Then, suddenly, when the Lord of Day reached the highest point of the sky—
He was addressed again by that great ascetic with words full of poison:
"O son of a minister, a night-stalker named Bhīṣaṇānana dwells here;

Therefore, without merits, can even a single night be spent in happiness with you, O Lord of this world, as one desires?
(Līlā 217) And here is the Sun, the sole witness to the deeds within the entire expanse of the universe...

The mountains, their peaks turned tawny by contact with the evening glow that is as orange as the twilight,
appear like golden statues set within groves of trees at their borders.

The clusters of forest *serihas* move about as if having just bathed. (Līlā 221) Among all the days, only one is praised:
that day upon which, from birth until now, separation from one another has never been seen. (Līlā 222)

Or rather, what is the use of much lamentation? In this world, even for the virtuous, heart’s desires do not indeed come to fruition without merit. Thus I speak to you, while this sun still has a portion of the day remaining.

Then he spoke again: "Enough with this talk; O Great-Minded One, that thief did not describe his character in such a manner.

He was difficult even for the foremost gods and celestial beings to conquer in battle during the night.
Here nearby is a place exceedingly enchanting, with beautiful flowering creepers and trees laden with fine fruit, its boundaries resounding with the cries of various birds.

A grove for the ascetic practice of the daughters of the yakṣas and maharṣis, where the clusters of sunbeams are incessantly obstructed by the sprouts of various trees—[this is] the pleasure garden of the lord of the yakṣas.
Therein dwells Mahānumatī by name, the beloved daughter of the lord of the yakṣas. *Līlāvatī* 2.29. Therefore, there... [she resides].
Seated in the hermitage of the ascetics, we do not know for what purpose [they are here]. Līlā. 230.

Thus, for these two whose minds are bound together by the bonds of mutual affection,
the days pass in the shared experience of equal joy and sorrow.
(Līlā 232) Therefore, come, before the vision of these eyes, whose appearance has changed, is obstructed.

Then the king arrived at that penance grove garden along with him, seeing which even the lord of the gods forgets his own abode. (Līlā.

It seems to be extinguished by the power of the spray from the waters of the great river, augmented by the frost, and by the gusts of wind from the grove of lotuses planted in front; thus it follows along the southern direction of that Kanakadevālaya temple. (Līlā 242)
Delightful as the speech of the Godāvarī river, [he saw] the charming Madhavī grove.

"Seated comfortably on a non-leaking seat, these are the Yakṣas' daughters.

Before his lotus-feet, while he was seated upon a comfortable throne, [she offered] him the water for washing the feet (argha). Līlā 249.

Having observed both of them, O King, it was reflected upon by my heart:

It is known here that she is the one and only Śrī, emerging from the foam of the ocean churned at that very moment, yet remaining without ornaments;

The beauty of that young girl was, as it were, gathered together by her breasts.

"A region where the heart is cooled is [far] from these [places].

"Stay for just a moment, enjoying the pleasure of a discourse on the Dharma.

Even though you speak harsh words with a mocking laugh toward your elders, nevertheless, your heart—having lost all remembrance [of her]—is quickly lightened by love. Therefore, if there is no distress in your mind, then tell me: what is this? (Līlā 267–268)
"Of such a kind is her wealth and status, of such a kind is the beauty of her form, of such a kind is her practice of penance,

especially so regarding one's own joys and sorrows, virtues and faults, as well as one's private intimacies. (Līlā 271A)

To people who do not know one's character and nature, what can be said, and how? (Līlā 272) Nevertheless, if you wish to hear it, then listen: there is a dwelling place of the happiness of the gods, known throughout the three worlds as Meru, the first among the great mountain-kings. (Līlā 273)
Whose feet are circumambulated by the sun’s horses, their limbs agitated by the dust raised from chariots stumbling on the gravel-strewn rocky slopes;
whose hooves are reddened by the fresh friction against the horns of the bull of Śiva. (Līlā. 274)
There, the lords of the quarters dwell together without any mutual fear;
there, pairs of Siddhas, seated comfortably upon the surfaces of golden rocks shattered by the thunderbolt-like talons of Garuḍa, drink nectar as they desire. (Līlā 275–276)
In the charming gardens where the peacocks perform their dance toward the six-faced one (Kārttikeya),
the hosts of Kinnaras sing with minds intoxicated by the nectar of the wind (Māruta).
(Līlā 277) There, the sound of the conversation between the swans of Viriñci (Brahmā) is heard intermingled [with other sounds].
Mixed with the sap of the *saptarṣi* and *śyāmā* plants, along with *tumburu* and *laktaka*, [the wine flows] in a stream made soft by the nectar of the well-opened *pārijātaka* flowers;
thus, beloved women, longing for union with their lovers, proceed swiftly upon that path. (Līlā 278–279)
Where the Goddess of Fortune alone attains her full splendor through golden lotuses, which are made radiant by swarms of bees drawn by the scent of the ichor flowing from the bathing Airāvaṇa;
in that mountain of the heretics, on the southern slopes, [there lies] the city complete in prosperity. (Līlā 280)

There was a city named Sulasā, which surpassed even the abodes of the lords of the gods. (Līlā 281) Therein dwelt a lord of the Vidyādharas named Haṃsa, renowned among the deities; his beloved wife, who followed his heart’s desire, was named Padmā. (Līlā 282)
Born from her [womb], she has two beautiful daughters who are lovely to behold: one is named Vasantasirī, and the second is Saradasirī.
(Līlā 283) Both of them are made happy by the wholesome instructions received from their elders.
The days pass for those who have no desire to worship the gods.
Thus, on Mount Kailāsa, before the Lord of Gaurī, their mastery in the art of the lute continues to flourish as they gain further renown. (Līlā 284–285)

his broad chest was dappled by the lattice of rays from the jewels on the hoods of the lord of serpents. (Līlā. 286)

Resounding with the clamor of swarms of bees greedy for the abundant ichor flowing from his temples; terrifying to those who bear weapons raised by trembling hands due to the suddenness of his action; and whose face is made formidable by the sight of serpents fleeing, their heads raised high, at the sound of his roar—Līlā.287–288.
With the broad frontal globes covered by a circle of fresh *pāriyātra* sprouts and blossoms,
emitting a loud roar produced by the striking of his tusk-tips,

With the multitude of his attendants stationed on one side of the mountain that was pressed down by the weight of his body, [he stood].

(Līlā 301) When [you become one] among the Vidyādharas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and humans...
"Then you shall behold the lotus-faces of those who have come together from all sides.
(Līlā 302) "At that time, O daughter, having cast off your sorrow, you shall regain your status as a Vidyādharī.
When this was said, the young girl vanished from sight. (Līlā 303)
Furthermore, the venerable one was addressed by the village headman: "O lady, do not weep;
by my favor, you shall obtain even that boon desired by your heart.
(Līlā 304) Thus, although she had obtained the boon, [she remained] in her own home due to the separation from her sister.

"O noble son, the young woman has gone weeping, full of sorrow because of her sorrows. (Līlā 305) Having seen her from afar, Ruirī informed her mother-in-law and father-in-law, as well as her kinsmen and elders, about everything that had been said by the mouth of Gaa. (Līlā 306)

Having heard that, with his arms outstretched, the swan replied with a clear echo: "Alas! That lord has not acted appropriately, in that he [has abandoned] that innocent princess whose intellect was blossoming in her childhood. (Līlā 307)
The dog was placed above even by the leader of the Gaṇas, though he knew [the truth].
Or rather, it is not his fault; this is the ripening of the fruit of a misdeed committed impulsively, appearing under the guise of the sorrow of separation from the beauty of autumn. (Līlā 308–309)
Having spoken thus for a long time, her face—its cheeks pressed by her arms and resembling the orb of the moon obscured by thick clouds—was addressed by her wife:
"O dear one, why do you grieve over this sorrowless tree? (Līlā 310)
Whatever is destined to happen occurs exactly so through the power of destiny (devayoga). (Līlā 311) But that which was improper was pursued by us with deluded hearts;
for that reason, we have obtained such a result this very day. (Līlā 312)
All maidens indeed are praised as long as they remain virgins in their family homes and have not yet become young women; it is not at the onset of fresh youth that they are so esteemed. (Līlā.
313) Therefore, to whom shall I give Vasantasirī, whose specific virtues have been truly witnessed?
Even a left-handed man goes to the left, as long as he has not been struck down by fate. (Līlā.

314) Furthermore, for people in this world of living beings, a husband who is desired by the heart is not found even for a moment; such a husband is difficult to find even for maidens throughout the three worlds. (Līlā. 315)
Having lamented thus many times, Sulasā’s husband was seized by a grief characterized by the failure of his specific increase in wealth due to his anxiety over the means of obtaining the boon.
(Līlā 316) Then, seeing him with a dejected face, his grief growing from the failure of the means to obtain the boon—
Having seen this, Vasantasirī reflected thus in her own heart:
"It is because of my fault that my father bears such a burden of anxiety, his heart overwhelmed by the sorrow arising from his deep affection. (Līlā 317–318)

So what is the use of this ill-conceived marriage ceremony? All such auspicious occasions belong only to those who are happy. (Līlā 319) Who laughs, who sings, who dances, and who indulges in sexual pleasure?
"Deprived of Sarasvatī’s splendor, this marriage of ours is joyless. Līlā:
320. "Nevertheless, maidens are indeed not independent; or rather, enough!
I shall act without anxiety regarding them, according to the word of Hēraṃba. Līlā: 321.
That which was spoken at that time by the compassionate Lord Gaṇeśa, the time for its fulfillment has now arrived through this desire for a bridegroom.
(Līlā 322) Therefore, what is the use of further deliberations? Let Nalakūvara be the bridegroom.

"O Lord of Wealth, by your grace, may my longing for the face of the maiden be fulfilled. (Līlā 323) Then, that longing for Dhana’s daughter suddenly arose in the heart of Haṃsa, whose face was blooming due to the power of the boon granted by Heramba. (Līlā 324)
Out of affection for his friends, kinsmen, and retinue, that lord of the Vidyādharas gave his own daughter, Nalakūbara, to him in marriage. (Līlā.
325) And by his father, the Lord of Wealth, he was also given [wealth] with great joy.

Having been accepted many times, she was received like a garland of flowers. On another day, Nalakūvara, moving along the sky which was filled with the splendor of the banners of various celestial chariots, suddenly arrived at Sulasa’s abode.
There, surrounded by a multitude of gods, siddhas, kinnaras, vidyādharas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, and with auspicious songs being sung, Sumati was married. (Līlā.
328) Then, having completed the wedding, [he set out] with the speed of those whose sole focus was on the journey to the bridegroom’s home.
By means of a multitude of celestial chariots, whose bells jingled with a sweet sound, he reached his own abode;
while he was dwelling there in happiness according to his desire, this daughter named Mahānumati was born to him. (Līlā 329–330)
"What does she say? Even though she was born into the Dhana family, despite such a state of affairs, she experiences this great suffering, which is contrary to her own nature. Līlā [says]:
"You yourself surely know that among all those women with faces smelling of sour milk..."
The days pass in the family home as they please, enchanting the mind. (Līlā 332) Salutations to you, O childhood!
You are praiseworthy in every respect—remaining as you were, wandering as you did, playing as you pleased, speaking as you wished, and acting however you liked. (Līlā 333)
Because of this, even she does not grow weary of wandering day after day with her circle of friends through regions as enchanting as a cluster of golden lotuses, enjoying herself as she pleases.
On another occasion at the end of the night, she said to me: "Dear friend, it is unprecedented... [Līlā 334]
"O King, since that is so for us, why then do we not go there?
Having sported together with the daughters of the Siddhas upon the swings of the Malaya breezes in the groves of mādhavī vines climbing the peaks of Mount Candanaruci, we shall return. (Līlā 335–336)
And I said, "Dear friend,
there is another region even more charming with its many virtues than this Alakāpurī.
(Līlā 337) [This was spoken] by her whose heart’s affection had increased through the confidence born from our intimacy on that very day.
"O friend, I say that even one's own birthplace is like heaven;

nevertheless, if you still desire to go to the Malaya mountain—which is enchanting with its dense groves of *lavalī*, *lavaṅga*, *elā*, and *nāgavallī* vines, and whose caves are filled with the waters of the ocean. (Līlā 338–339)
"Know this: even the sun bears the splendor of the consort of the Lord of the Gods;
therefore, let us go before all the pleasure-gardens are crowded. (Līlā 340) Then, from her celestial chariot, she immediately descended along with her circle of female companions.
With their rows of bees scattered by the wind in the courtyard of the sky,
the leaves reached the Malaya mountain— the mountain that fills the face of the southern quarter with its own vastness and serves as a precious ornament for the shore of the ocean. (Līlā 341–342)
Having burnt the world, it stands as a massed heap like the fire of universal destruction, its hips flashing with the sun and thick smoke-veils of darkness clinging to its peaks;
[it is cooled] by the waters of its cascades, made cool by contact with sandalwood, camphor, and cloves. (Līlā. 343)
It acts like a cooling breeze for the ocean ablaze with the submarine fire.
(Līlā 344) The mass of stars, swirling amidst the clusters of rocky plateaus, endures the shadows cast by the spray flowing from waterfalls shattered by the fall of massive peaks.
(Līlā 345)
Where the rays of the sun do not enter the groves of leafy trees—groves where pairs of bees, intoxicated by the nectar of the flowers, hum at the end of their songs—they seem to feel ashamed;
[there, the trees] are resorted to by female serpents who have cast off the poison of their expanded hoods. (Līlā 3.46)

The trees, which serve as perches for the swans of the nearby sun, are being fanned by the breezes from the Kalpavṛkṣa trees, which are shaken by the garments of celestial women as they pull at the flowers with their hands—[thus it is] with the Siddha couples.
(Līlā 3.47) And also: [the breezes] that cause the *palāśa* flowers to bloom.
[The mountain] where the breeze is pleasantly cool, wafting from the swaying branches of sandalwood trees;
where masses of grass emerge, their ripeness revealed by the water trickling down from the slopes of emerald peaks;
and where the natural streams are discernible by the smoothness spreading over the surfaces of crystal slabs. (Līlā 348–349)
Where crowds of sages sit comfortably, refreshed by the spray from the waters of the clouds;
where the expanse of the sky is concealed by peaks, obscuring the light of the ten directions;
and whose borders are fashioned by various charming gardens, golden palaces, and rows of lotus ponds—thus [is it]. (Līlā 350)
Līlā. 351. [He beheld] Mount Malaya, the exceedingly enchanting abode of the gods and the Siddhas.
Līlā. 352. And on one part of the slope of that great mountain, he saw a magnificent pleasure-grove, made beautiful by the fragrance of the flowers of many kinds of trees, which perfumed the air.

Resounding with the humming of bees mingled with the loud cries of various well-praised birds, it wafts the fragrant scent of blossoms opening from the mouths of bees at its entrance; it possesses a slow-moving enclosure of betel-nut clusters embraced by the fragrance carried by the wind. (Līlā 3.53)

Where the thickets of *kaṇi* creepers hang down near the sacrificial posts (*vaiveḍha*), their roots drenched by the flowing sap of *pauṛa* fruits crushed by the multitude of monkeys; where the God of Love is worshipped with *puṣpalāi* flowers placed at the foot of the trees.
It was a mountain garden, enchanting like the palace of the Moon-god, its interior filled with the rays of the sun and various rows of creepers and tender shoots.
In its center stood a mansion with a courtyard paved with variegated jewels. (Līlā 3.56)
Seeing which, even the gods become disenchanted with their own homes.
(Līlā 357) In front of that palace, upon a charming jeweled floor, a single young girl was seen sitting comfortably, like the very splendor of a garden grove. (Līlā 358)
There, as she lowered her neck in modesty while looking at us with eyes cast down from her lute, our aerial chariot stationed in the path of the sky was perceived by her.
And she spoke, her heart’s sincerity accepted through a prostration with joined palms: *Līlā 359* And she spoke, her heart’s sincerity accepted through a prostration with joined palms.
Rising up with unshakable modesty and sweet words:
"O blessed ladies, behold this garden-palace, which, by the service of your own lotus-feet, possesses a beauty like that of the Nandana grove. (Līlā 360–361)

Then, having first entrusted our hearts— which were overflowing with the emotion expanding from the joy of her words— to him, we slowly entered the palace. (Līlā 362) And there, O noble son, we took possession of a comfortable seat.
She asked the young woman: "O beautiful one, tell me, who are you?
Whose is this hand, so laden with various and diverse patterns of leaves? And to whom do these two excellent lutes with their sweet sounds belong? (Līlā 363–364)

To whom do these variegated woven cloths belong, inscribed with patterns that suggest the totality of every art? To whom do these appear, which delight by shattering the pride of the haughty? (Līlā 365)
O beautiful one, these various weapons are smeared with sandalwood paste. (Līlā 366) To whom does this appear to belong, O gentle girl, at the edge of the lake?
And to whom does this excellent palace belong, resembling a book and appearing like a dwelling for the God of Love? Tell me. (Līlā 367)
Having heard that from me, she spoke again out of affection: "O Blessed One, listen if you have such curiosity regarding this:
here is a city with well-constructed walls atop the peak of the Malaya mountain. (Līlā 368)
Fragrant with the scent of the blossoms of many trees reaching to its very limits,
its layout graced by the playful splendor of the lotus-faces of hosts of Siddhas, the great city named Kerala is desirable even to the gods. (Līlā 369–370)
There, like the Lord of the Suras, the Lord of the Siddhas known as Malānila was renowned throughout the three worlds; like Mount Meru, his position was unassailable. (Līlā.
371) His first wife, who followed his heart’s desire, was named Kamalā.
She has but one beloved kinsman, named Mādhavānila.
This garden, a dwelling for the sciences, was fashioned for him by his lord Mālayānila, whose heart is bound by affection for his dear sister. (Līlā 372–373)
"I am here his garden-keeper, named Mādhavīlatā;
we have played together in the same dust since birth, and with him alone.
Having heard this, Līlā said to her: "Noble son, you are blessed!"
"Such is the attainment of a master in the abode of Malaya. (Līlā 375) Having spoken thus, Mādhavilā said again: "Blessed one, you too must instruct us:
who are you, whose life has been made fruitful by us? (Līlā 376)
And she told me, "O beautiful one, we too have gone to Mount Malaya out of curiosity for the pleasure of swinging. Then, with her eyes and face blooming with impetuosity, she spoke to us. (Līlā 377)
"There he is on the swing; enjoy yourself as you wish right now! [Līlā 378] Then Mahānumatī suddenly said to her own female attendants:
"Swing yourselves there until it becomes our turn. [Līlā 379]

The swing is rocked by young girls whose singular state of being has been uprooted by the longing for the first agitation of love; it is as if the God of Love himself were being swung during the festival. (Līlā.
380) By a certain beloved who was yearning with the desire for her first union...
Overcome by love, he acted like a lover on a swing.

Having intoxicated her—who was longing for the pleasure of lovemaking—he enjoyed himself with her in such a way that he became someone to be especially desired for love-making even by others many times over. (Līlā 381–382)
Līlā said after a long time: "O Vārōsārandoli, we too have enjoyed ourselves here as much as we desired; now you also enjoy yourselves.
Therefore, O brother, we too shall play there for a long time according to our desire.
Seated right there once more upon the lap of the jeweled pavement— Līlā 384—
just as we were about to set out on our return journey after resting for a mere moment,
that Siddha-kumāra suddenly arrived from that very place. Līlā 385.
Then, saying "This is he," the Yakṣa maidens verified him with great curiosity for a long time, using every means possible.
Then, while being verified by those young women who had previously experienced passion at first sight, Līlā.386... [the verse continues].
Līlā.387: He has come near me, together with Mādhavilā, into my presence.
Līlā.388: Then, having offered a prostration from afar, he was addressed by me there:
"O brother, may you have your desires fulfilled; live long together with your kinsmen."
And he said: "O Blessed One, whatever you desire, let that surely be so for us;
today all our auspicious omens have come to pass. (Līlā 389) "Today, O Noble Lady, she has achieved her goal—she who was difficult even for the Lord of the Gods to overcome."

"The ground is marked by the royal insignia of your lotus feet. (Līlā 390) While he was speaking thus, Mahānumati suddenly beheld his face there with her eyes turned toward him, accompanied by a longing glance from her tremulous eyes. (Līlā 391)
Mahānumatī was repeatedly gazed upon by that curious man with eyes that turned and rolled at the very limit of their range;
and she, in turn, was seen by him as her eyes met his with a playful and tender grace. (Līlā 392)

Having seen the beauty of Mahānumati’s form, [the king] was overcome with passion. (Līlā 393) Therefore, even though he was already handsome, he became exceptionally beautiful with his throbbing grace, like the body of a flowering creeper adorned with young shoots. (Līlā 394)
Her eyes, instantly filled with streams of tears and bathed in the water of despair, became like blue water-lilies (kuvalaya).
A radiance spreads from her pupils, shimmering within the expanse of her wide-open lashes.
Her gaze is as tender as a young tree of the bliss of her heart's desire.
(Līlā 396) Her breasts repeatedly turn upward;
they are distinguished by the sighs of fear, as if for the purpose of lifting up the lotus-face of her modesty. (Līlā 397)

With their garments disheveled by the agitation of their own sighs and fluttering unevenly, their straight breaths reveal their pair of breasts as if for the sake of being seen; their limbs, thick with the contact of a spreading net of horripilation, endure— Līlā 398.
