The spray of sweat glistens upon her, flowing over her three-fold folds of skin that are as fragile as waves; it appears like the outpouring of the water of beauty from her breasts, which are heavy with loveliness, as if its qualities had been poured forth through every limb and released at the end.

Her gaze, its power to resist suppressed by the shame of her friends gathered around, turns back in exhaustion, pushed aside by the god of love; even for that youth, its forward momentum is checked as it is perceived for but a moment’s blink. (Līlā 401)
The pair of eyes, whose hearts were protected from the pain of separation, met [in union].
(Līlā 402) Then, trickling down like the essence of the nectar-moisture of the moonlight of her face, love—as it were—sprouted over her entire body under the guise of horripilation. (Līlā 403)
The eyes of both, restrained by a courageous resolve to protect one another’s modesty,
throb with a longing for a gaze that remains unfulfilled.
(Līlā 404) The first sight of both was marked by a fresh, tender, and playful charm that overflowed with the power of passion.
"My heart is indeed tossing with desires for a union that wavers.
[Līlā 405] Having perceived this very thing, I said to my friend Mahānumatī:
"Friend, the day is turning; O gentle one, what can be done? Why this delay in departing? [Līlā 406]

Having spoken thus, we two, who were mutually enamored and straightforward in our intentions, remained standing by each other’s side with our hearts elsewhere. (Līlā 407) Then I too said to him: "Prince, this day has come to its conclusion."
Who can measure the nectar-like bliss of beholding you?
(Līlā 408) Blessed are those for whom you are visible day and night;
by your coming here today, even this birth of ours has become fruitful. (Līlā 409)
Therefore, you must now act in such a way that our mutual affection, which has been cultivated through your coming and going to our dwellings, may continue to increase. (Līlā.
410) Here, we are accompanied by those who are like great venomous serpents, experts in the art of deception.
"The path will become difficult to traverse when the sun has set. Therefore, fear has entered my heart; dismiss the day, O Prince, for some time remains for us to deliberate. (Līlā 411–412)
And he said:
"O Blessed One, in this world of living beings, a conversation free from suspicion occurs only between certain fortunate souls.
Therefore, enough with further talk; that which has been told by you is sufficient for us. (Līlā 413)
Therefore, you have done well; do not fear the venomous serpents now.
(Līlā 414) Indeed, O Blessed One, this Malaya mountain was formerly a place difficult even for the gods to traverse, its sandalwood forests obstructed by great poisonous snakes.
(Līlā 415)
Having realized that [the world] is difficult to protect,
my father overstepped the sandalwood groves of the realm of the Siddhas and propitiated Garuḍa;
therefore, O noble lady, he gave me this ring named Nāyikā.
"Seize them, so that those venomous serpents do not prevail over you in the sky. (Līlā 417) "Let alone those sky-wanderers;
even for the nāgas who dwell in the subterranean realm, their poison is destroyed by this [man] standing at the gateway of his sight. (Līlā 418)

And I said: "O Prince, listen! This one, brought from hand to hand by this princess, shall be the destroyer of all poison. (Līlā 419) Having heard this, [he was] with tears of joy mingled with the water of a bashful face...
In her heart, she laughed—a smile whose true nature was concealed by the suspicion of being observed.
(Līlā 420) Then, with her left hand, which was eager for the pleasure of his touch and equal in size, she pressed his right hand. (Līlā 421)

He slowly inserted his finger between my little and ring fingers in such a way that we both laughed inwardly at one another. (Līlā 422) Then, by the coolness arising from the touch of his hand— like that of the moon— ...
She became as if fashioned from water and joined together by moonstones.
(Līlā 423) Then, as passion was unfolding, her body—exquisitely adorned with various charms of that moment—was as if constructed from nectar. (Līlā 424)
Then, supporting that *mādhavī* creeper at her throat as she trembled with agitation, she was addressed there by the noble son:
"Friend, what shall we say? Together with you, we are beyond all means of remedy. (Līlā 425)

"Even so, you speak thus; once, you must prove me true. (Līlā 426) Then, by means of many words full of affection and persuasive in their artifice, there was nothing that Mahānumatī did not say to her. (Līlā 427)
And she said: "O Mistress, do not speak thus;
my very mind is longing for the sight of your lotus-feet, so why do you reproach me?
(Līlā 428) As she was speaking thus, she firmly clung to her neck.

She thought, "That Siddhakumāra has embraced me. Then, having been gratified by words that brought joy at his arrival at the festival, she gave him her brother’s necklace of large, pure pearls. (Līlā 429–430)
Having thus bid farewell to Mādhavī there, she set out toward her own aerial chariot together with her entire retinue.
Even though she was urged by her companions, she did not move from that spot for a moment. (Līlā 431)
The gaze follows her retreating mind;
[she moves] as if momentarily held back by bees clinging to her feet, their faces closing in apprehension at the thought, "Do not go! (Līlā 432–433).
As she ascended to her celestial chariot, I too, having taken my leave of that prince for a long time,
suddenly mounted the chariot.
(Līlā 434) With eyes darting to protect my heart, I turned them toward the direction [in which she had gone].
Enough! We have somehow reached these women with their faces covered.

(Līlā 435) Just then, the sun, its strength exhausted by the burden of tears shed from the exhaustion of traveling across the vast expanse of the sky, went to the peak of another great mountain king. (Līlā 436)
Having ascended the path of the sky, the sun has surpassed the gaze of people;
even those who are great, when their self-composure falters, succumb to defeat.
Though setting, the sun is indeed supported on the crest of the western mountain.
Even the sun becomes beloved by the people in his final stage.
(Līlā 438) The mountain of wealth bears the solar orb like a golden lotus, with its surrounding rays as slender stalks and its intensely reddened corona as half-formed filaments. (Līlā 439)
Even the orb of the sun, though worthy of being seen, has become difficult to behold like a pair of wild elephants in rut;

it is red with the clusters of flowers from its wide-open rays and smiles. But now, gradually, it descends, tossed by the waters of the ocean shore. (Līlā 4.40) Furthermore, it recedes little by little.

The sun, like a mass of sparks produced by the force of the wind obstructed by the thunderbolt, [fades]; and the twilight, thick with its descent, has burst forth in the sky like the radiance of jewels revealed by the waters of the ocean shattered by the falling sun. (Līlā 441–442)

The twilight, resembling the sap oozing from the trunk of the Lord of Days as he falls upon the stone of the western mountain— his strength slackened by the transformation of time, like the fruit of a tree struck by lightning—
is now enveloped by a sparse radiance of twilight intermingled with thinning darkness. (Līlā 443) It has become [thus].
The sky is dark red, its cheeks stained by the unbroken clusters of *śyāmā* creepers.

(Līlā 444) The glows of the quarters of the horizon, turbid with darkness mingled with the dust of the earth, seem as if they are being dragged down by the weight of the sun’s orb as it sinks at the end of the day. (Līlā 445)

The sky was illuminated by darkness, which, like a black balance-beam, bore on its tip the weight of the sun’s orb as it was being crushed by the heavy jaws of the hour; meanwhile, the face of night possessed the luster of saffron slightly reddened by the waters of the earth. (Līlā 4.46)
It endures the spreading mass of darkness,
which is like a swarm of bees that has taken flight as the broad lotus of the day withers at the close of twilight, its petals still slightly clinging together. (Līlā 447–448)

When the sun has reached its decline, the sandalwood tree of the sky withers like a plantain tree struck by its own internal disease; it is as if a black venomous serpent, in the form of darkness, has bitten it. (Līlā.
449) Now that the lotus-forest of the sun’s heat has closed, the night-lotus of the shimmering stars has blossomed.

The sky, which had become like a lake with the water of the darkness seen at dawn, has now become like a pool. (Līlā 450) The sky is completely shrouded by the darkness, which is like the smoke of the submarine fire rising from the path of the ocean waters shattered by the falling sun. (Līlā 451)

As if fashioned by water-laden waves or constructed by swarms of bees, a mass of darkness—dark as the throat of a *kalakaṇṭha* bird—has arisen and spread; it makes the expanse of the sky appear like molten iron and the quarters of the horizon as if smeared with collyrium. (Līlā 452)
This forest thicket, dense with trees, has become as it were a single expanse of light.
(Līlā 453) Then there appeared the first shimmering, expansive, white radiance of the moon’s chariot-pole, as he was still hidden behind the mountain peaks.
(Līlā 454)
At the edge of the mass of darkness, the light of the very tender moon is seen like the water of the milk-ocean remaining after the churning by the Great Boar lying upon his bed.
[Līlā 455] It bears the mottled appearance of being licked by the upward-turning, shimmering, and sparse rays of the moon.
Like the Vindhya mountain with its mass of darkness and its cascading torrents of tears, [the eastern quarter appeared];
then the eastern direction arose, sprinkled by the rays of the rising moon, reddened like the eyes of a female serpent enraged by a peacock. (Līlā 456–457)
In the meantime,
having dismissed her entire circle of female attendants, she entered her dwelling, her limbs tormented by the blows of Love’s arrows.
(Līlā 458) Meanwhile, I too— with a heart trembling from the anxiety over her long delay— [arrived].
She has come to rest at the feet of her mother, Vasantasirī.
Līlā was addressed: "Daughter, why have you even avoided your own home today?
Tell me, where did you enjoy yourself, or where did you wander for so long? (Līlā 459–460)
It was told to me by my mother today that in Malaya, while we were sporting in a grove of sandalwood trees,
Mahānumati climbed to the top of a mādhavī creeper hanging from the peak of a sandalwood tree and played on a swing.
(Līlā 461) That she has not come to the feet of you two until now.
Her limbs were exhausted from the fatigue of long swinging.
Having heard this, I was sent by my mother to that very place;
however, she was not seen by me there in the bedchamber.
I have reflected deeply: who is that woman, her limbs tormented by the arrows of Love, who remains even without us? Or rather, what else could it be?
(Līlā 464) For thus is the bed, with its unevenly curved indentations from the movements of her lifeless body.
And so here, the entire courtyard was strewn with heaps of flowers.
(Līlā 465) Thus, from her couch she went to the floor, from the floor back again to the couch;
and from the couch, she ascended to the palace, which was cool with the rays of the moon. (Līlā 466)
Having reflected thus, and pondering it many times with a heart overcome by affection, I ascended this jeweled palace.
(Līlā 467) Meanwhile, [the moonlight] being pierced by the rays of the moon situated upon the peak of the rising mountain...
That mass of darkness enters the interiors of the mountain caves. (Līlā.
468) Adorned with the flowers of the stainless stars, the swan of the moon, its wings outspread as rays of light, enters the sky-lake from the peaks of the mountain of the moon. (Līlā. 469)
With rays extending like long lotus stalks, the deer-marked moon drinks up the mass of darkness situated within the lake of the intermediate space between the worlds.
(Līlā 470) Thus do the moonbeams tell us that they are burning with fire during separation from their beloved.

In the courtyard of the house, the lotus-pond, with its lotus-faces closed, is like a woman whose face is turned away. (Līlā 471) Thinking, "Affection becomes most difficult to endure through this [moon] which has the nature of appearing only rarely," the lotus-pond has become averse to the company of the moon.
(Līlā 472)
Having gazed upon that moon, which is like a revolving furnace for the great arrows of love, I have reflected in my heart: "This [moon] is a poison for separated women.
(Līlā 473) Then, there, I saw her, her limbs scorched by the unbearable arrows of Love.
Immediately embraced by the contact of her lap against the mosaic floor inlaid with precious stones, [she was recognized].
Having approached her side and, overcome with emotion, caressed her limbs with her hands, [Līlā] said: "Dear friend, what kind of person is he?"
"Friend, why have you left that bedchamber there and come here to the touch of the crystal floor inlaid with jewels?
Or is it because this garden breeze, cool with the mass of gathered flowers, [is so pleasant]? (Līlā 476)
O dear friend, while smelling [the flowers], you even forget to breathe.
(Līlā 477) Or rather, upon hearing the thick humming of bees intoxicated by drinking many flower-nectars, you suddenly lift up your body as if startled. (Līlā 478)
O dear friend, why do you remain motionless even during the cool season, your limbs scorched by the rays of the moon that surpasses the mass of snow?
(Līlā 479) [She who is] overwhelmed by confusion, with her agitation subsiding only through the lingering sighs released in anxiety.

"Why do you make your speech falter with such repetitive utterances? (Līlā 480) O dear friend, why do you speak these disconnected words—this reply whose syllables and meaning are indistinct—fearing that they might be overheard by the attendants nearby? (Līlā 481)
Why, moreover, do you gaze with unblinking eyes, unable to fix your aim, as tears well up within you, suppressed by many various thoughts?
(Līlā 482) Your lotus-face is drenched at its very roots by the water falling from your arms, which are raised halfway and rendered disheveled.
"Why do you bear a face resembling the orb of the moon risen at dawn?
(Līlā 483) Why, O bee-like eye, do you place but a single drop of collyrium upon the slope of your breast, which is already tawny with the pollen of fresh lotus filaments? (Līlā 484)
"Why do you hide from me this pain felt in your own heart?
When it is spoken of, it becomes light; when it is not spoken of, it becomes heavy.
(Līlā 485) Then, having heard this from her, [he saw] her pair of eyes reddened with shame.
"What has been said is not to be denied; how much less so that which is entirely untrue?
(Līlā 486) "O dear friend, that which was done by the maiden of a family restrained by modesty—something unworthy—is now undertaken by my heart with even greater intensity. (Līlā 487)
"How indeed will you tell it? Or how will you not tell it?
Even though it is impossible to accomplish and has been guarded for a long time, it must nevertheless be told to you; therefore, listen.
(Līlā 488) Having seen that Siddhakumāra, these wicked companions...
We have been led onto a path of immodesty by our own eyes; what can we say?

(Līlā 489) O dear friend, although you know this is utterly contrary to the state of maidenhood, nevertheless, through the power of the god of love, I am placed at the forefront of those who are shameless. (Līlā 490)

O friend, that Garuḍa, laughing, bestowed upon me even without cause such a grace that destroys the poison of all serpents; O dear friend, it is precisely this greatness of his magnanimity that I bear in mind. (Līlā 491)
Loving her as she grew up, and constantly reflecting upon her affectionate nature,
her character, her lineage, her disposition, her learning, her modesty, and her many other virtues, [the mother] has fallen into a state of immodesty. (Līlā 492–493)

Therefore, even you here, having failed to speak out and having lost all sense of sincerity through shame, have reportedly climbed onto this [tree] which is cool from contact with the moonlight and the breeze. (Līlā.
494) Therefore, by these things difficult to behold, resembling sharp saws and razors...
O friend, the quarters have been especially cooled by the moonbeams, as if by the scoundrels. Līlā. 495.
Today these quarters are as if set ablaze by the moonbeams; even the breezes in the garden today come as if smeared with poison. Līlā. 496.
"Tell me, dear friend, in what state does the fever of those women—who are like fuel for the great fire of love—come to an end?
It is the state of the limbs of those who have committed evil deeds.
And I said, "Dear friend, others also say exactly all this."

This intoxication of love cannot be guarded against by any means. (Līlā 498) But that other [intoxication] can be hidden; however, O gentle one, this secret of the God of Love, when it is being revealed, does not become so manifest as it is while it is still concealed. (Līlā 499)
Having spoken thus, O brother, I prepared a bed with lotus petals like unto you, cool with camphor, sandalwood, and water-lilies.
Yet, O noble youth, her fever did not find any relief through that either. *Līlā*, 500.
Having looked toward the south with great fear, I—Līlā—then [beheld her].
O noble son, that Mādhavī creeper, her lotus-face momentarily withered by the exhaustion of traveling through the sky, suddenly arrived. (Līlā 501–502)

Having greeted her with great haste, I was embraced first by me and afterwards by her, whose limbs were covered in horripilation born of affection. (Līlā 503) Then, that bed, where sprouts were fashioned by the tossing of her arms—
Having seen her, the Great God of Love was first praised by Māhavilā;
then, the crest of the celestial tree’s blossoms and a palm-leaf fan were presented to her lotus-face by the messenger of her beloved. (Līlā 504–505)
Then he, whose majesty was attained through contact with the lotus-hands of this beloved, was suddenly placed upon my breast by her, who was filled with joy.
And then he too was [received] by me, whose face and eyes were suddenly blossomed with delight. (Līlā 506)
That letter was sent by the messenger at the urging of my own words. (Līlā 507) "Hail from the city of Mālava, O beautiful one!
Your Mādhava’s wind writes this letter with its full meaning;
what need is there for much [else]? You should reflect upon it. (Līlā 508)
"Even by this necklace, cool with the pleasure of contact with her fresh breasts,
the fire of love pervading all your limbs cannot be extinguished.
Having heard this, the five-arrowed god [Kāma], to whom she offered a silent salutation with joined palms, [acted].
With her heart alone, she bowed to me, whose eyes were like bending blue lotuses.
(Līlā 510) Then, by Mādhavilā, the message from the prince was told to me:
"O Mother, King Mādhava respectfully requests this of you. (Līlā 511)

You are not an object of mere formal courtesy, nor are you merely the subject of common worldly talk; nevertheless, I truly say that no one other than you is the doer of what is dear to us. Līlā. 512.
That alone is a good moment, that alone is a fortunate day, and that alone is the light of beautiful eyes.
"That moment will soon pass when you shall be seen by me once again.
(Līlā 513) And I said, "Friend Mādhavīlatā, tell me, for what purpose was the God of Love so highly esteemed by you? To which she, her mind likewise bewildered, replied: (Līlā 514)

And she said: "O Blessed One, by this [favor] the prince also spent the day in that very place, his mind intent on recounting your virtues. (Līlā 515) Therefore, may the exhaustion of the day be allayed by the pleasure of contact with the shadow of the mountain of wealth.
The sun was embraced by the western quarter, overflowing with passion for her.
(Līlā 516) The rows of trees became thick with the lustre of various flocks of birds perched upon their crests;
they were draped in dense darkness that oozed from their trunks like soft, clinging sap. (Līlā 517)
The expanse of the sky has suddenly become like a forest, scorched by the fire of twilight, set ablaze by the stars as if by brushwood, and darkened by the blackness of gloom.
(Līlā 5.18) With all the faces of the quarters extinguished and the beauty of the world withered away...
Suddenly, as if swallowed by the interior of the night’s darkness, the surface of the world seemed devoured.
(Līlā 519) Then, with the splendor of the frontal globes of a rutting elephant submerged in a lake, the orb of the moon rose, its lower half crimson. (Līlā 520)
The moonlight of the young moon, whose orb is slightly reddened, spreads forth with a glow as tawny and crimson as the plumage of the *surasundarī* bird.
Like a thicket of *tamāla* trees broken apart by the mass of foam from the ocean agitated by Mount Mandara, [the darkness vanishes]. (Līlā. 5.21)
The darkness becomes agitated by the shimmering, sparse rays of the moon.

(Līlā 522) The sky is seen with its surface jagged by the delicate rays of the crescent moon, its dense darkness pierced through, and it possesses the luster of a floor of emerald slabs reddened by the glow of a lamp.
(Līlā 523)
Behold, the path of the sky appears like a black serpent whose slough has loosened slightly, being pierced by the rays of the moon situated upon the peak of the western mountain.
Meanwhile, the masses of darkness are being sprinkled by the pale, aged rays of the moon.
The quarters of the sky have become like the shores of the ocean of milk.
(Līlā 525) The night-lotuses, accompanied by swarms of bees greedy for the fragrance exhaled from their slightly opened petals, burst open as if filled with darkness pierced by the moon. (Līlā 526)
The rays of the sun protect the remaining darkness—driven out by the crowding together of the rays—as if they were refugees who had fled to mountain caves;
for he has extinguished the entire world with his universal, all-pervading heat. (Līlā 5.27)
The lotus, failing to achieve union with the moon, was indeed deceived.
(Līlā 528) Therefore, in the heart of the prince—which is tender with the flavor of passion for a person difficult to attain—the moonbeams have entered like flower-arrows. (Līlā 529)

Then that prince, as if bearing the poison of the fragrance of full-blown, excellent flowers, sat down right there upon the ground, which was like a pit for you; though overcome by unbearable torment, he remained greedy for the pleasure of touching her feet. (Līlā 530)

Seated with her entire body [bent over], she does not desire even a bed of lotus leaves. (Līlā 531) The moon is carried away by the night, and the night by the moon; by both of them, Love is carried away;
by Love, too, her separation is carried away; and by that separation, her torment is carried away far away. (Līlā 532)
That necklace was placed upon her heart, which was already tormented by the discharge of the arrows of Love;
it was cast around her like a noose by Love, who had discharged his shaft.
(Līlā 5.33) Today, by this merciless night-stalker, she has been seized as if by a demon.
In an instant, her limbs were reduced to nothing but skin and bone.
Then, gazing for a long time with unblinking eyes at that which had lost its mark, he supplicated the moon, the wind, and the garden itself. (Līlā 534–535)
"O Moon, O Wind, O Garden of Paradise, protect the limbs of my beloved— limbs as delicate as the filaments of a fresh lotus— from my heart!
(Līlā 5.36) Having heard that, I suddenly said, "Prince, enough of this!"

“Where is that beloved when such incoherent things are being said? “Why have you forgotten yourself, that you speak what is untrue? In time, loves that are difficult to obtain do come to pass. (Līlā 537–538)
Moreover, it is heard here that the state of passion (*kāmāvasthā*) is indeed manifold;
it gradually ascends upon the body of the lover. First, there is the delight of the longing ignited by mutual glances. (Līlā 539)
Even a conversation arises between lovers through some pretext. (Līlā 540) And immediately following the course of that conversation, anxiety settles in the mind;
as it is being contemplated, Love spreads forth, bearing his bow strung with living energy. (Līlā 541)
Having discerned the course of affairs through the words of messengers, hearts filled to the brim with the longing of conjecture make their gifts and receive them. (Līlā.
542) The extraction of virtues is not fully contemplated by a heart satisfied merely by the arrival of a messenger.
On that day, he was praised by his friends together as one who never tires of [her virtues].
(Līlā 543) I wonder to what is that reunion comparable, which is free from doubt for couples who have heard the praises of her qualities and are filled with longing? (Līlā 544)
That other, seventh rasa, which brings relief to every limb and is expected to be even dearer than the first union with a beloved, is not heard of in the treatises;
it is beyond the reach even of great poets. (Līlā 5.45)
Whatever pleasure a lover provides in a new union, such is the joy of their meeting;
from that joy arises mutual longing, from longing grows affection, and from affection, devotion increases. (Līlā 546–547)
When a wager increases in stakes,
whatever deception occurs through some stroke of fate— that is the unbearable transformation of love.
But you, on the other hand, have reached such a state here merely by being seen.
"O friend, you have become overwhelmed by the torment of the great fire of love.
(Līlā 549) Then he said to me: "O talkative girl, say this:
'Have you not come within the range of his gaze—those glances that are languid, slow, and tremulous with half-closed eyes? (Līlā 550)
"If you remember even a single word that was said by her to you, then go;
do not speak in such a manner from now on. Having spoken thus, O Blessed One, I was dismissed by him here. (Līlā 5.51)
"Now that I have seen it, I shall depart for the fourfold mire of your feet.
(Līlā 552) And I said, "O beautiful one, tell this repeatedly to your master in my name, so that he does not entertain any other thought. (Līlā 553)
"You are said to be a scion of Malayanila, whose feet are touched by the crest-jewels of all the renowned Siddhas;
you are born from a noble mother. And Mahānumati here—you yourself surely know the family into which she was born. (Līlā 5.54) You too [know her].
What remains? Only that which is taught by the conduct of those who possess the wealth of poetic expression.
Therefore, in this world of living beings, such a mutual correspondence of the splendor of knowledge among those whose very nature is merit occurs only for a few. (Līlā 5.555–556)
"Having persuaded Niśāntaka, let this maiden-jewel be chosen with all care; it is a source of joy even for those who delight in the pleasure of play.
(Līlā 5.57) And then Mādhavilā said: "O Mother, as for what you say..."
Just now, the goddess said something as a message to her husband.
And Mahānumatī, her face slightly averted out of modesty, said:
"O dear friend, you are too straightforward; what do I know of sending a message? (Līlā 558–559)
"From you comes my happiness; from you, sleep; from you, my life and union with my beloved.
Do whatever you deem best. (Līlā 5.60) Having thus understood her purpose, that female messenger departed from our presence.

We too are intent upon grasping the multitude of her virtues. (Līlā 561) Then, with her gone, the fire of the bodiless god (Aṇaṅga) has blazed up even more intensely in her heart, obscured by the dense fog of manifold thoughts and imaginings. (Līlā 562)
Then, after she had been made to breathe for a mere moment by her friend, whose gaze was motionless due to suppressed breath, she spoke:
"Friend, that which was told to Mādhavilā, and that by which we have been instructed— " Līlā 563.

Not a single word was spoken by him that was worthy of her. (Līlā 564) "May no other suffering, even more intense than this, befall me as I carry a heart tormented by the fault of having been rejected. (Līlā 565)
"Therefore, with my mind agitated, come, let us go to Mount Malaya;
friend, I shall give myself to him of my own accord.
There is no more endurance for delay, for my heart is set ablaze by the fire of love. (Līlā 566)
"Even his life has been heard by you to have fallen into a state of doubt.
Līlā said: "And my dear friend, I have heard, seen, and personally experienced the misdeeds of the flower-weaponed god (Kāma); what more can you tell me? (Līlā 567–568)

Driven by certain past deeds, this wretched person, desiring happiness, falls in love with one whose affection is difficult to obtain. (Līlā 569) For those lovers who are agitated by the longing for a rare union, such is what happens.
May Ananga burn with that very suffering of one who watches the calamity of another.

(Līlā 570) Those by whom the beloved was never known are the first among the happy, for they have never experienced the pain of separation; know that those for whom there is indeed separation from the beloved are the first among the miserable. (Līlā 571)
Fortunate are those who do not taste the flavor of loves that are joined in suffering, broken in an instant, harsh in their conclusion through separation, and difficult to fulfill.
(Līlā 5.72) Nevertheless, do not grieve, do not despair, and do not abandon yourself.
Who gives and who takes away? Or who [bestows] the pleasant and the unpleasant? Whatever has been ordained for whom, that shall be so. (Līlā.
573) In such a way that virtues flourish, the retinue and the people become devoted, and the elders offer praise—in that manner should such a task be performed. (Līlā. 574)
Those actions which are bitter at the outset but sweet like nectar in their result—when well-considered, they do not bring laughter upon people.
Therefore, my dear friend, I say: whatever maiden in this world acts according to her own will... [Līlā 575]
She is worthy of being gazed upon by the lords of the world, especially by those like us.

(Līlā 576) The daughter of Nalakūbara, born from the very essence of the splendor of spring—how, my dear friend, could you possibly bring reproach upon yourself through such a transgression? (Līlā 577)
One's own self is given away by one's own self only to those who are free from possessions and restrained;
for maidens born of noble families, this path simply does not exist. (Līlā.
578) Why should I tell you that I myself have experienced this very same thing?
"Listen with attentive hearts, dear friend, to what has been increased by the occasion.
(Līlā 579) There was once a king named Viśvāsaka, who was the lord of the earth girdled by the four oceans under his sway, who had destroyed the hosts of his enemies.
(Līlā 580)

He, the lord of men, who for a long time dwelt upon the path of his sword—the very abode of the goddess Earth, the primordial beauty of the quarters, and the victorious glory of the three worlds—was not satisfied with that singular fortune of the universe. (Līlā. 581)

Having bestowed his entire kingdom upon the gods, he departed for the slopes of the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya), where the air was perfumed by the blossoms of trees sprinkled with the cool frost of the celestial river's waters; there he began to practice great austerities. (Līlā 582–583)
There, for an incalculable time, subsisting on roots and fruits with a body at peace,
having the nature of a deer or a bird, clothed in bark, sleeping on rocks, dwelling in leaf-huts, and free from attachment— he practiced asceticism there. (Līlā 5.84)
Thus commanded by the Lord of the Gods out of fear, the celestial nymph Rambhā said:
"O Rambhā, go and create an obstacle for the eminent sage Vētāsaṇa, who stands within the forest thicket and whose heart is devoted to fierce asceticism. (Līlā 585A)

The excellent sage, whose limbs were suddenly thrilled with joy, reached the dense forest where he had previously performed his penance; there, as soon as the mind of that noble ascetic was stirred by the sight of the celestial nymph, the fire of passion [blazed up].
Līlā 585B. In that mind of the noble sage, which was moved by the sight of the celestial woman, the fire of love...

She blazed forth, drenched with the fuel of delusion and eager to burn away her impurities. (Līlā 585) Having remained with him for some time, her mind infatuated by passion, she became pregnant; thus she whose husband was satisfied became one who had pleased the Lord of the Gods. (Līlā 586)
I am the one born from the womb of Rambhā, Tisrā, the beauty of the three worlds;
she abandoned me at the time of my birth and ascended to heaven. Līlā. 587.
And then, dear friend, my father too, considering me to be deprived of my mother—
The forest deities there offered me every comfort.
Then, having been nourished by them with the nectar-like juice of fruits, I eventually became free from illness and was able to wander about in that penance grove. (Līlā 588–589)
Clad in garments of bark and cotton, wearing loincloths as their only covering, she reached the joy of childish play together with the deer-keepers.
After some days, I was released from that state of childhood by him. (Līlā 590)
My mind has turned toward the practice of asceticism in this heat and mire.
(Līlā 591) I shall bring various roots, tubers, and fruits produced by the trees; I am content with the work of sweeping, sprinkling, and cleansing. (Līlā 592)
At another time, at the end of the night, [he saw] a forest of trees with blossoming trees, lusting after the flowers of various excellent branches;
its directions resounded with the cries of noble birds, and its groves of trees were made to sing out with the humming of swarms of bees intoxicated by honey. (Līlā 5.93)

Where the rays of the sun are incessantly screened by the sprouts of the creepers on the kalpa-trees; where the tips of the branches of the *vaccha* trees are bent down by the weight of their succulent fruit and kiss the ground;
and whose borders are drenched by the frost from the mountain streams on the peaks of the Himālaya. (Līlā 594–595)
With its stone slabs polished by the many feet of the gods and its surface shimmering with red lac,
where throngs of other bees are driven away by the humming of the scent-eaters— such is this forest, my dear friend, frequented by him out of his longing for flowers. (Līlā 5.96)
When I had approached her, who was unaware of the turn of events, she laughed;
then, there, with her heart overflowing with affection manifested by the offering of fragrant flowers, she spoke the truth, her hand reaching down to the stream of the Vāmanaka river. (Līlā 597–598)
Dispelling the tumult of the falling dust, it possesses a halo of glorious splendor;

its celestial path is made resonant by the sound of small bells swaying in the wind; and it creates a multitude of rainbows through the radiance of various excellent gems that flash forth. (Līlā 5.99)
[She beheld] a celestial chariot descending from the sky, a realm of bliss.
(Līlā 600) There, [he saw] one whose body was adorned by the burgeoning onset of early youth, with flower garlands and ornaments hanging down from his broad chest. (Līlā 601)

With the interior of his heart perfumed by the moisture of perspiration flowing from every limb under the influence of a gentle breeze; with the forest of his entire body drenched by the radiance of his loveliness; and with his face resting upon the lotus of his playful gesture, where bees are manifesting as the pupils of his eyes—Līlā. 602.
Hearing my words, the divine youth approached.
(Līlā 603) Then, seeing him, I—my heart moved by his state of being—respectfully offered a handful of flowers before him as a sign of wonder. (Līlā 604)
While I was reflecting in my heart, today these eyes— filled with longing and seeing the world of their beloveds fulfilled— have seen him.
(Līlā 605) Then, having approached me, that curious man asked:
Līlā: With words that are soft and sweet-syllabled, you speak with sincerity.

O friend, in this grove of new golden *kadamba* trees, where the swarms of bees humming like a lovely sound [reside], who are you that wanders fearlessly and without hesitation, enjoying the delights of the celestial nymphs? (Līlā 606–607)

Having heard that, my dear friend, I first uttered words that were pleasing to him, [revealing] his own residence, family, and name clearly. Then he [responded] with longing, joy, agitation, and respect. (Līlā 608)
I spoke again, full of longing, affection, and playfulness:
"O beautiful one, let us meet alone without hindrance, since I too have been born into a pure family of Gandharvas. (Līlā 609–610)
But your heart has been captivated by the longing to see you;
if you become gracious, then what was done by the God of Love will be justified.
Today’s day [is won]—the kingdom, the treasury, life, happiness, and the body [are all yours]. (Līlā 6.11)
Whatever else I possess, all of it belongs to you.
(Līlā 612) Therefore, look upon me with favor and give me your sprout-like hand; do not delay, for the love that has blossomed in my heart cannot endure any further waiting. (Līlā 613)
Thus, having heard those words so sweet and full of significance, our hearts, filled with the ocean of emotion, have suddenly blossomed.
(Līlā 614) O friend, [our hearts] are moistened by him through tears of joy that fill them.
As if pierced by her very eyes, she who could not remember a reply— Līlā—
by means of sighs that issued from her mouth wide open due to the force of an intoxication of extreme apprehension, herself revealed the innermost state of her heart. (Līlā 615–616)
Līlā: "Because my limbs were unsteady, I was unable to endure it; with words faltering from shame, I disclosed the true state of my heart.
O dear friend, what is there that has not been betrayed by the rising of goosebumps?"
Her pride was diminished by her laughter and her thighs trembled;
thus, with her limbs blooming in this manner, intoxicated by love, the modest and virtuous Guṇamati cast aside her sense of propriety. (Līlā 618–619)
As she was scratching the surface of the earth there with her left big toe, she spoke in a low voice with her face cast downwards:
"Friend, who does not praise him? Or for whom would he not cause delight? (Līlā 6.20)

"How is it that you are not bound [by love], or how is it that you do not see [it] from me? (Līlā 621) "O noble one, if you desire me even knowing me to be a forest-dwelling ascetic, then go to our penance grove and speak thus to her. (Līlā 622)
Then he spoke again: "Enough of this! Why do you delay so long?

Love in my heart, overflowing with the joy of beholding you, cannot endure it, O lady with eyes like blue lotuses who have dwelt for so long in another's presence and have missed the opportune moment. (Līlā. 623)
"Thousands of obstacles beset a heart’s desired undertaking.
(Līlā 624) Having spoken thus, he—his lips and hands trembling with emotion—seized my hand, knowing the desire of my mind, and drew it away. (Līlā 625)
Therefore, my dear friend, that marriage was suddenly completed by me through the intoxication of passion,

Speech that is concise yet rich in meaning, endowed with sincerity— O Līlā,
when will that auspicious day come, when your eyes, now fixed without blinking due to the exhaustion of anxiety, shall attain the bliss of nirvāṇa through the sight of him? (Līlā 968–969)
And they said: "O brother, may he live long;
may that day endure wherein Līlāvatī experiences the bliss of union with the lotus-like beauty of his hand. (Līlā.
970) [This was said] upon obtaining the consolation of news regarding her own body sent by her beloved.
"Congratulations, dear friend! thus was Līlāvatī addressed by them.
With their minds overflowing with the joy and bliss of mutual delight, they beheld that necklace which lay upon Līlāvatī’s neck. (Līlā. 971–972)
Then, with faces dejected by the sudden onset of the pain of separation from her beloved, they said:
"Friend Līlāvatī, this necklace looks beautiful upon your breasts.
The Queen replied: "This was brought here by Vijayānanda."
Hearing this, she spoke with her eyes fixed upon my face: "Līlā.974 Where did your master obtain this necklace that brings joy to your science?
And for how long has it been kept within the treasury of Hāla? Līlā.975
And it was told by me: "O King, that lord of men named Vīravāhana, the ruler of Mount Malaya, has been captured by us in divine battle.
(Līlā 976) As his great treasure was being presented by the king himself...
"Having searched the ocean, this excellent necklace has been sent.
(Līlā 977) Having heard that [message], which was as unbearable as the impact of a thunderbolt, both of them wept so much that even Līlāvatī fell into a swoon. (Līlā 978)
Alas! Why did he not grow weary while taking such a course?
For he placed that necklace upon his heart, even though it was burning with the unbearable fire of love.
(Līlā 979) Alas! Why have I remained thus for so long, cursed by my own ill fortune?
My life was preserved by this wicked woman out of mere sport. Līlā. 980.
Having reflected upon that indiscretion in my heart, I placed it in the hand of Mādhavilā; how indeed has it been cast away? Līlā. 981.

Alas, O you whose heart is hard as adamant! Today, at the sight of the pearl necklace, our hope for union with the prince has burst forth; O Kuvalayāvalī, that we did not die at that very moment is the fruit of this [sight]. (Līlā 982)
"O Līlā, go now; you have endured this extraordinary misfortune with great grace.
This very calamity has been borne by us through our own fault;
for us as well, this is the end of our stay here. (Līlā 983–984)

O fawn-eyed one, preceded by Vijayānanda, your departure toward the presence of the King, who is overflowing with passion, shall be endured [by him]. Having heard that [news], O Lord of Men, which was as unbearable as the blow of a thunderbolt... [Līlā 985]
Līlāvaī, her flow of breath faltering, remained unconscious for a long time.
(Līlā 986) I thought within my heart: "Alas! O cursed Fate, what is this right of yours?
Is it fitting to exert yourself in destroying everyone at once? (Līlā 987)
The Yakṣa maiden said: "Since I sent the necklace to you, I am now sending these rings as a reciprocal gift.
That which belonged to me was then handed over to him directly, hand to hand. (Līlā 988)
"His very destiny is now that of this finger-ring.
(Līlā 989) Having spoken thus, O Lord of Men, he himself has sent this ring as a return-gift for the Yakṣa, dispatched with great effort to you. (Līlā 990)
And she said, pressing her lotus-face close to my ear:
"Send Śālivāhana to my presence at once, so that even he who has captivated her heart may have it snatched away from her without restraint. (Līlā 991)

"How indeed could she desire death upon seeing him face-to-face? (Līlā 992) "Therefore, I shall hand over Līlāvatī here into his own hands, and afterwards I will carry out the endeavor for the purpose desired by my heart. (Līlā 993)
Having spoken thus, I was suddenly dispatched there by that Līlāvatī; then she said, "O dear one, listen:
you must say to my lord, 'Of the joys of beholding your lotus-feet... (Līlā. 994)
"May I not have such a birth again in another life.
(Līlā 995) Thus, having surrendered all my possessions, I have now come to the root of your lotus feet, which are free from the grasp of worldly attachment. (Līlā 996)
"O Lord of Men, whatever is appropriate for such a matter as this should be done without delay, in accordance with my instruction.
Having heard that for a long time, O lady with eyes like blue water-lilies, that king at that very moment—
As if established in meditation, as if bewildered in mind, or as if deceived, he became motionless, his eyes devoid of light and his power of movement lost.
Vijayānanda said to him: "O King, enough with this delay here. (Līlā 998–999)
Do what was whispered by Mahānumati so that it may be accomplished;
who knows the course of events? Even in this way, things somehow turn out. O King, even though you were not present in her mind, Kusumālikā [was won] by you.
"How is it that she, who has increased the pleasure of seeing you, desires death? [Thus spoke] Līlā.
And then the Lord of the Earth said: "Do not speak in such a manner;
for our beloveds do not have hearts like those of ordinary people. (Līlā 1001–1002)
"Believe this: even that which is spoken in jest by those who live in such a manner comes to pass; but what is spoken with sincere intention cannot be otherwise. (Līlā.
1003) "He himself does not believe me, and I too do not wish for him today—what has happened?"

With the death of Mahānumatī, our own death too would be pleasant. (Līlā 1004) Even if we were to die there, it would be together with them; therefore, it is better that it be known right here, as having a conclusion free from deceit. (Līlā 1005)
If, by means of a life as flickering as the tongue in the mouth of a serpent,
one can obtain the occasion of death in this world of living beings, then who among those dying would not be satisfied? (Līlā 1006) That which was commanded for him by some incorporeal voice—
"I shall tell a lie in this world, but the truth in the next.
(Līlā.1007) Having understood that the King’s mind was thus agitated by the hope of union with Tilōasundarī, the preceptor Nāgārjuna spoke to the lord of the earth: (Līlā.1008)
"Ho! Śrī Śālāhaṇa, why do you speak in such a manner—like a base man, a speech devoid of the quality of great magnanimity?
Those things in this world which lead neither to Dharma, nor to Kāma, nor even to Mokṣa... (Līlā. 1009)
The arising and destruction of men is like that of blades of grass.
(Līlā 1010) Birth is for the sake of death, and death is solely for the sake of birth;
there is nothing else but this for those of evil intellect wandering in saṃsāra. (Līlā 1011)

Furthermore, O King, those who do not abandon their lives attain other incomparable perfections in this world of living beings through right reflection. Do you not know that in *saṃsāra*, every being that has gone [to death] has indeed gone [to its end]? 1012. *Līlā* 1012.
"Where can I find one who will bring me together with my dear friends? (Līlā 1013) Therefore, what is the use of this fruitless death that follows the path of base men?
If you do not desire the kingdom here, then come; let us go to Pātāla. (Līlā 1014)
"Remaining there, O Lord, the brave men from heaven dwell for countless thousands of years, free from the affliction of old age.
Having heard this, the king, whose eyes were like those of a young deer with wide-open pupils— Līlā 1015.
Having reflected for a long time, he accepted the words of the monk. Then,
on another day at dawn, having transferred his own kingdom to his son, the king set out,
weary of the pursuit of worldly pleasures.
Valuing that very thing highly, his heart filled with dissatisfaction at death, Nāgārjuna departed from his own city by means of a stratagem involving Nāgārjunā. (Līlā.
1018) [He endured] the unbearable [grief] of the feudatories, ministers, servants, kinsmen, friends, and the common people.
Causing distress, he approached the bank of the Godāvarī river.
(Līlā 1019) Accompanied by two hundred princes on each of his two sides, the king set out together with one hundred poets.
(Līlā 1020)
Preceded by the mendicant Nāgārjuna, the king, stationed on the riverbank,
proceeded toward the cave together with Vijayānanda.
Then he beheld [the cave] along with his very dear and steadfast companions.
Having reached the opening whose entrance was guarded by the lion-king,
they all now advanced toward the great lion, disregarding the fear inspired by the hissing sounds emitted from his wide-open, gaping mouth. (Līlā 1022–1023)
Then, with a mere glance, he shattered that second gate-section— which was constructed upon a broad stone foundation and guarded by a host of Ganeshas—
just as the mountain of Kapāla-pura became free [of obstacles] upon the removal of the three defects. (Līlā 10.24)
Then, as they were traveling along the road, they saw Bhavānī’s grove— Līlā 1025—
a forest thicket of trees perfumed by the fragrance of Bakula and Lavalī groves, and shaded by the vast canopies of Aśoka, Viśāla, Sāla, Piyāla, and Tāla trees. Līlā 1026.

Abounding with *puṇṇāga*, *nāga-kesara*, *keāi*, *kaṅkēlli*, and *kuravaka* trees, and filled with *kunda*, *kuruṇṭaka*, *kuñjaka*, *kañcana*, and *kaṇavīra* flowers; [it possesses] a thicket of young mangoes, beautiful *campaka*, sandalwood, and *devadāru* trees. (Līlā 10.27)
The fragrance of fresh jasmine and *mōa* flowers mingling with the scent of *mandāra*, *uddhamāla*, and *mallikā*;

the surface of the earth carpeted with the petals of blooming white *sinduvāra*, *pāṭala*, *piyaṅgu*, and *nōmālikā* blossoms, and strewn with the fallen petals of opened white lotuses. (Līlā 1028–1029)
A forest thicket where trees are set ablaze by the humming of swarms of bees intoxicated by honey;
its entire perimeter resounds with the warbling of cuckoos; delightful with the unrestrained and magnificent prosperity of the excellent *aśvattha* and *udumbara* trees bearing fruit—Līlā. 1030.
O deer-eyed one, such is the garden of the temple of the God of gods, delightful with *suha*, *māhuliṅga*, *nāla*, *ērī*, *kēli*, *dakkhā*, and *hirāmaara* trees,
beholding which the lords of men attain great perfection (*mahāsiddhi*). (Līlā 1031–1032)
Having praised that beloved of Bhavānī, who brings about the state of existence,
for a short while, O fawn-eyed one, just as they were proceeding forward,
the third door appeared with its golden panels wide open. (Līlā 10.33)
