And it was said: "Aha!
Behold! This Great Being, desiring to enter the underworld, remains bound by wicked serpents.
(Līlā 1036) O fair lady, while the lord of men was speaking thus, all those venomous serpents—
Leaving that youth, they fled toward the ten directions.
Then that excellent youth exclaimed: "Well done, well done, O King!
Who else besides you here is capable of destroying the calamities of others?"
The wise man is not conquered by you; there is no one else like you who benefits others, for here is seen one whose kindness is without cause.
(Līlā 1039) Therefore, what shall I say to such as us, who have cast off our worldly attachments?
"Whatever has been and whatever will be—all that shall be entirely yours.
Having said this, the King asked: "O you who have performed good deeds, what is there that cannot be accomplished through you? Therefore, tell us: what do you yourselves require? (Līlā 1040–1041)
And he said: "O King, please sit down; I shall relate it in great detail.
To whom else should my very self be told by me?
(Līlā.1042) There is [a place] whose navel is enchanting with the symphony of the various cries of many kinds of birds...
Its slopes are perfumed by the fragrance of cloves, nutmegs, cardamom, and sandalwood;
its rocky surfaces are reddened by the lac-dye from the feet of celestial women;
and this great mountain named Malaya is a dwelling place of bliss for the Siddhas. (Līlā 1043–1044)
There dwells a renowned lord of the Siddhas named Malayanila;
I am his son, O Lord, known as Madhavanila, equal to the Wind-god himself.
Having heard this, the king, with eyes like those of a young deer gazing upward— Līlā 10.45. a. Then, having heard that from the lord of men...
He compared his own self to one made happy by the attainment of the glory of the three worlds.
And he said: "O noble hero, this is that very ring; by the sight of it, you shall be instantly released from these bonds. (Līlā 1046–1047)
Then, seeing that finger of his suddenly, the Siddha prince, his heart overwhelmed by a mixture of joy and sorrow, exclaimed:
"Līlā.1048 Where was this excellent finger obtained by you, O Lord of the Earth?"
"O friend, what a great marvel this is! Where has he come from here?
(Līlā 1049) And the lord of the earth related to him the entire account of Mahānumatī, whose beauty was like the petals of a blue lotus, as it had been told by Sāgara. (Līlā 1050)
Then, with eyes and face blooming with joy at his bowing, he said:
"Even so, why do you still linger here?
For even after such a long time, those venomous serpents who were formerly our enemies—" [Līlā 1051]... [remained as they were].

"I was bound and remained here, yet that very necklace fell upon one of great virtue. (Līlā 1052) Then indeed, that necklace, which had been placed far away from me by kinsmen fearing enmity, has become the foremost among virtues. (Līlā 1053)
"Go now;
I too shall depart from the city of Mālava and join you after I have settled my elders in a secure place.
Having spoken thus, O deer-eyed one, toward King Mṛgāṅkadatta, who was headed for the Malaya mountain—
Overwhelmed with supreme bliss, the Siddha youth departed suddenly.
(Līlā 1055) Then, having opened that golden door, two women with moon-like faces approached the slender maiden in the presence of their lord. (Līlā 1056)
There they said: "O Lord of Men, enter this excellent palace of Ratnaprabhā;
our mistress is distressed because of you.
Having heard that, the King spoke his own words to Nāgārjuna. *Līlāvatī*, 1057.
Having entrusted the ocean to their speech, they spoke thus: "Līlā.1058 This is exactly as you say regarding the excellent palace of Ratnaprabhā, which is difficult to obtain;
however, there is one further thing that must be said. Līlā.1059"
"This friend of Mādhava’s, the breeze, is not yet completely at ease;
therefore, it is not fitting for us to remain here in this manner.
Having spoken thus, those two female messengers were dismissed. (Līlā 1060)
Having paid homage to the Lord along with Nāgārjuna, the king departed;
he reached his own city surrounded by all his subjects, bathed in the waters of the Godāvarī river, and entered his palace. (Līlā 1061–1062)
A celebration arose in every single house of all the kings when the lord of the earth was seen, having arrived at his desired goal. (Līlā 1063) Then,
by the watchman stationed at every post, [it was announced] suddenly...
"The rule regarding the consumption of cow's milk has been granted by the Lord out of satisfaction.
(Līlā 1064) Therefore, with my heart filled with the resonance swelling forth at dawn, and with my throat overflowing with increasing joy, I have quickly wandered about.
(Līlā 1065)
"Prepare the pack-saddles, yoke the oxen, and have the fodder-troughs cleaned for the horses in the stable at Pallāṇa.
Let five hundred rutting female elephants be driven out. (Līlā 1066)
"Let some of the council members remain here, and let others depart.
Let Agnimāna lead the Raṭṭhauḍa forces in the rear; let Sulakṣaṇa go with the master [the king] and the troop of cavalry through the middle. (Līlā 1067–1068)
"Send him who has been bound by the decree;
at dawn, together with the porters and excellent carriers, you must have the palanquins prepared.
(Līlā 1069) While this clamor was spreading openly, at that very moment on the mountain of wealth...
The sun has swiftly departed, bound by his many duties in the western quarter.
The rays of the lamp-like sun shine, gleaming within the city mansions like beams released by the sun to measure the extent of the darkness. (Līlā 1070–1071)
Then the moon, like a crest-jewel atop the mountain-king of the eastern peak, like a lordly elephant warding off the host of darkness, and like a horse with many distinct faces, ascended high.
Then he who had long been accustomed to waking at dawn, having bestowed his command upon all his subordinates... [Līlā 1072]

The lover has approached his own respective dwelling; [yet] some man, bewildered by pride, approaches the proud woman. Having transferred his heart to her, the husband stands nearby, close to her confidante who understands her gestures and facial expressions. (Līlā 1073–1074)

Her face shines, with its cheeks moist and radiant from suppressed laughter, its eyes wide open and rolling as if in bloom, even though her lover is faultless and she herself is longing for a passionate embrace. (Līlā 10.75)
Even for some, pride—which is difficult to subdue—is brought down by the power of love.
(Līlā 1076) The whetstone for pride becomes dull from the excessive joy of incessant amorous play;
yet, love becomes fresh once again. (Līlā 1077)
Even though he was intent on his religious observances, a certain lover was forcibly embraced by a certain smiling woman and kissed,
even as his face was turned away by a grunt of protest. (Līlā 1078) Even though his heart was elsewhere, a certain man was [embraced] by a certain woman whose cheeks were flushed with excitement...
One who is unable to provide a bed for you is carried off by a lover who acts perversely.

(Līlā 1079) Another beloved woman, weary from many nights of lovemaking and no longer desiring even her husband, holds him fast by force under the pretext of an embrace, even though he has only half-risen. (Līlā 1080)
Moreover, at that time, their conversations were filled with the sweetness of love, bound by the circumstances of their meeting;
as they massaged each other’s limbs, horripilation spread over them from the joy of the touch. (Līlā 10.81)

The beauty of their lotus-faces was enhanced by the horripilation caused by the sudden release of a single glance; their words were being softly understood through eyes that rolled within the corners of their lashes; and they were enchanting with the tinkling sounds emitted as their nails brushed against one another’s faces. (Līlā 1082)

With their limbs moistened by the spray of sea water and their bodies softened by the coolness of the sand, these [pleasures] are bestowed upon couples— pleasures whose connection to incomparable bliss is known only through mental conception,
whose intensity increases, and which are utterly enchanting. (Līlā 1083–1084)

The couples sleep through the remainder of the night with their limbs rubbed together by the exhaustion of the sudden onset of deep sleep, as they stir restlessly; the pairs of lotus-eyes of the couples become closed by the weight of profound slumber. (Līlā 10.85)

His eyes were like doors fashioned for the protection of the treasure within. (Līlā 1086) Then, heralded by the songs of bards and made manifest by the morning chants, there arrived the dawn of the king, bringing the joy of his long-cherished vow to depart. (Līlā 1087)
The expanse of the sky has become pale yellow with a slight tinge of dawn-red at its edge, turning white like the wings of a pigeon;
it is filled with the clamor of flocks of birds taking flight from their respective nests. (Līlā 10.88)

The forests seem to rise up, longing for a sight of the face of the Sun, the Lord of Day. (Līlā 1089) Shaken by the spreading morning breeze, the multitude of thin stars falls from the tree of the sky like a falling shower of water-drops. (Līlā 1090)
At dawn, when the bull has descended and the moon-bird has flown away, the white star-flowers of the night-lady are falling.
Having drunk the moonlight-liquor of the night-creeper, [the stars] are like crystal cups. (Līlā 1091)
The moon, with its bees settled upon it, descends from the sky.
(Līlā 1092) The clusters of night-lotuses close their petals, overcome by the joy produced by the pleasant morning breeze, as if out of fear of the approaching harsh-rayed sun. (Līlā 1093)
Like a lamp whose flame is overcome by the wind of the sighs of a beloved woman who has just woken from sleep,
the glow of affection fades when the intimacy has been enjoyed. (Līlā 1094) For couples who have risen after sleeping happily in a four-watch embrace...
The glances of those languid with the drowsiness of sleep are most precious when seen.

(Līlā 1095) The beds are released after a long time by the longing women, as if they were beloveds, with sighs heavy from their bodies turning languidly due to the lingering touch of sleep. (Līlā 1096)
Who is this woman, her broad silk garment slightly revealed by the loosened knot held in her trembling hand, who is being supported by the hem of her robe by her lover as she leaves the bed?
[Līlā 1097] The eyes of amorous women, languid with sleep and parched, are beautiful.
The gentle tossings of their heads, as they stumble over the lotuses used for decoration, shine upon the faces of the amorous women at dawn;
even though fashioned with every effort, their faces do not appear so beautiful at the onset of night. (Līlā 1098–1099)
Even with her speech silenced by the heavy drowsiness at the end of the night, she burns all the women with that half-glance from the corner of her eye.
(Līlā 1100) Her four limbs are exhausted and unable to bear the weight of her ornaments, and her disheveled tresses are indistinguishable from them.

The co-wives shed tears that possess the luster of the color of a blue lotus. (Līlā 1101) Now, when such a dawn had broken and the drum of the morning sacrifice was beaten, the astrologers informed [the king]:
"O Lord, this is an auspicious conjunction. (Līlā 1102)
Then the king, having performed the auspicious rites for victory with the sounds of divine musical instruments, emerged accompanied by a multitude of bards crying out "Victory!
Victory!", while the quarters of the sky were filled with the sound of hundreds of trumpets, conchs, *kāhalas*, and *ḍhakkās*. (Līlā 1103)
With the circles of his feet covered by the dust raised by the hooves of his elephants and horses,
O gentle one, the king has encamped near his own city, his lotus-like head sprinkled with the abundance of flowers offered by the lotus-hands of celestial beauties. (Līlā 1104–1105)
On another day, as the multitude of women being led away were bound with the entire force [of the army],
the herd of cattle, terrified by the clamor and outcry of the crowds of people, did not remain still, moving along the path that was equally uneven and level. (Līlā 1106)
Līlā 1107: The courtesan, her face distorted with confusion as she was cast down from the opening of the window, fell away.
Līlā 1108: As the young bull, terrified by the great elephant, fled, the nose of the camel, whose master was crying out in distress, was torn away along with the earth.
Someone else says: "Do not push it out! Do you not see the bull?
You will fall like Kōhala from the sweets; this is our Liṅgarua.
When the *karamba-aḍera* has been broken, whom will you seek here in this *hārī*? *Līlā 1109*
Do you not see the loads of merchandise crushed by the chariot?
(Līlā 1110) A certain rogue youth, supporting himself with one hand on his wife—who is herself a vessel of misfortune—goes along with the thief, being struck [by the chariot]. (Līlā 1111)
"O serpent, proud of your own beauty, do not shake this withered fruit in vain!
This is our new stallion, not yet saddled. (Līlā 1112) Having thus turned back the outcry by another woman who raised her hands in defiance.
As if by its own death, it has fallen before those who have already fallen.
Look, our cock has been devoured by that dog—a low-born beast with a voice like a Brahmin—who, with a laugh, has eaten his head while it was still full of life. (Līlā 1113–1114)
Another says: "Why do you breathe so hard on the noble steed in vain? Here goes a boar, bewildered by the strike of my arrow.
Thus, occupied with such mutual conversation, [the day] somehow reached its end. (Līlā 1115)
Khaṇḍāraka arrived at a certain spot on the slope of the Śailanī mountain. (Līlā 1116) Meanwhile, there was a collection of chariots whose horses were weary and whose axles were being rubbed smooth;
and there were laborers running after them, driven by the pursuit of harvesting fodder nearby. (Līlā 1117)

A multitude of constant lords who have begun the destruction of their dwellings, with the entire assembly of water-jars filled by the rut-fluid of elephants; [a place] filled with the sounds of distressed and wailing hands placed upon the heavy burden of exhaustion. (Līlā 1118)

Līlā.1119–1120: That valley began to serve as a dwelling for that mountain-hipped woman, who was clothed in the wealth of various forest regions emerging from within the groves; she was like an intoxicated female elephant, being gently led along the long path of the road by her own exhaustion.
The rays of the sun, appearing like dust raised by the army encamped there, seem to be approaching for the purpose of providing lodging and food to the multitude of troops;
meanwhile, serpents, agitated by the path of the marching elephants' feet, climb up. (Līlā. 11.21)
As if for the sake of surveying the entire world with their eyes, the chariots, their horses weary from galloping on the long road, release their lofty peaks;
their reins slacken as they are cast aside due to the horses' veering off course, and the aiming of the arrows becomes loose. (Līlā 11.22–11.23)
The swift horses, their saddles trembling as they gallop, are somehow steadied by the grooms who pull back their foreheads with force while they are burdened by heavy breaths;
their heaps of dust cling to them, moistened by the spray of sweat from the exertion of pulling. (Līlā 11.24)
Even when saddled, the horses carry heavy limbs.
(Līlā 1125) Intoxicated elephants consume with difficulty even a handful of sprouts, their thirst only slightly assuaged by the breeze spreading from the movement of their trunks. (Līlā 1126)
Struck by the breeze from the palm-leaf fans, they somehow regain their shape on the bed;

with the flow of sweat trickling down as they turn over and change position, [the marks] appear like uneven sesame seeds sprinkled by droplets emerging from the perspiration caused by the exertion of coming and going.
(Līlā. 1127) [The beds] possess uneven sesame seeds scattered by the droplets of sweat emerging from the exertion of moving about and sitting up.
The faces of the amorous women, with their eyes closed, are as precious as blossoms. (Līlā 1128) In the meantime, the hunters informed King Śrīsālavāhana:
"O Lord, the Susāva forest is being traversed. (Līlā 1129)
The eastern direction is crowded with many large and lofty compounds, obstructed by mountain ridges, and constantly blocked by herds of elephants;
likewise, the other [direction] is filled with bamboo thickets clinging to the branches near the slopes of the mountain ridges. (Līlā 1130)
"Quickly!"—thus was the northern quarter taken possession of by the guardians of Dharma.
In the western quarter, which is pleasant to traverse, excellent steeds were stationed;
in the southern quarter, a mass of tawny monkeys was deployed. (Līlā 1131–1132)
Thus, the king arrived at that very spot with his retinue, while the herds of deer were being driven away by the hunters.
At that moment, the forest deer, agitated by the sound of the hunters' cries, looked up in alarm. (Līlā.
Even without being struck, the doe, fearing my death, retreats;
the tiger retreats before the boar, and he too before the leopard, and he again before the deer—whom does such delusion of mind not lead to death? (Līlā 1134–1135)
The doe does not move, bound by the cords of affection for her newborn fawn;
and the deer, too, remains right there despondent along with his beloved.
(Līlā 1136) He who abandons his companion whose life is being snatched away by the sharp arrowheads...
By his own mind, he performed a deed corresponding to his name [Śikhaṇḍin].
(Līlā 1137) Even though he had flown far away, the peacock—having leaped over the multitude of elephants, horses, and men—fell into the mouths of dogs;
even death is better than being cursed by fate. (Līlā 1138)
Even though the circle of hunters was drawn up with their bows strung,

not a single arrow fell upon him as he stood equally desirous of both [the deer and the hunter], while the first arrow of the hunter, whose neck was bent low, struck the doe. (Līlā 11.39) vāvallullūriakandharassa paḍhamaṁ maassa hariṇīē...
By her heart’s bursting, life was abandoned as if for a committed offense. (Līlā 1140) By the blow [of his fist], Madhu died;
by separation, I likewise died; and the tears remembered by the housewife’s eyes also vanished from her arms—all three died at one and the same time. (Līlā 1141)
The herds of boars are being caught by fierce Śoraṭṭha dogs as they flee through mountain caves, their cries echoing off the peaks. (Līlā 11.42) Meanwhile,
[the lion] is joined by eyes reddened with indignation at the direct insult to his own kin.
Having struck down the men and horses, the boar approached the king.
Then that fierce boar, whose nature was skillful in leaping and turning, struck the horse of the lord of the earth, and by him [the king] also, that boar was struck. (Līlā 1143–1144)

Thus, having made even this forest devoid of birds in an instant, the king arrived at the fortress at the time of day’s end. Līlā.1145 He was addressed by Vijayānanda: "O King, do not delay here in vain."
"Who knows what kind of course events will take from now on? (Līlā 1146).
Having been addressed thus by him, that king, after many days had passed, reached the terrifying Saptagodāvarī, whose waters were as beautiful as lotus petals. (Līlā 1147)
Having completed his bath and meal there, with all his needs satisfied by the residents of that hermitage, his joy increased, and he was addressed by Vijayānanda:
"O Lord, this great sage here is our disinterested and sincere kinsman. (Līlā. 1148)
Mahānumatī remains in the penance grove because she was not brought back by you.

(Līlā 1149) To see that ascetic, whose youth has passed, who is distinguished by the wealth of his knowledge and noble birth, and who has set out upon the path to the next world—even for you, that will become [a source of sorrow]. (Līlā 1150)
And the King said: "Dear kinsman, what do you say? Come, let us go;
has he not done enough for us by doing even this much?
Having spoken thus, the lord of men—[she] whose eyes were like those of a young fawn with upturned lids— [Līlā 1151].
Vijayānanda was first sent by the Sage to [the Lord’s] presence. Having approached from afar with prostrations, he was received by the Lord of Sages;
seated nearby, he was questioned many times regarding his welfare. (Līlā 1152–1153)
And he said, "King Śrīsālavāhana is well;
longing for the attainment of the pleasure of seeing you here, he follows along this path. Then he replied, "This is that very King Sālavāhana."
The glory of him whose ten directions are sung by the beautiful goddesses is celebrated.
(Līlā 1155) Therefore, no rival whatsoever is seen for him here on this earth; for what purpose has he come here from his own city? (Līlā 1156)

Having heard all that he reported exactly as it was, that great sage, overcome with emotion, said: "What you have told us is indeed a cause for celebration, since some way or another, Mahānumatī’s heart's desire has been fulfilled today. (Līlā. 1157)

Līlāvatī too has become one who has fulfilled her own share of misfortune. (Līlā 1158) While such a conversation was taking place, the king also arrived there at the presence of those [princes], surrounded by a limited retinue. (Līlā 1159)

Then that great sage, having sprinkled the king with the water of the *arghya* offering, said to him, "Sit upon the lap of this comfortable throne. (Līlā 1160) Then, as he occupied the lion-throne, he was addressed by the eminent sage:
O Lord of Men, you have been proven true by us today.
Having lived for so long a time in this worldly existence without companions, even though we were [supposed to be] with companions, please now make us truly possessed of companions. (Līlā 1161–1162)
On this day, the gods perform a musical concert for Umāpati;
with those gone, O Lord of Men, the Rākṣasas sport during the nights.
Among them, there is one preeminent Rākṣasa named Bhīṣaṇānana. (Līlā 1163)
Out of fear of him, the community of sages does not dwell even for a single day.
Therefore, knowing that the battle with him will take place this very day at the hour of nightfall, let this mantra be received from me. (Līlā 1164–1165)
"May that unrighteousness by which you see the Rākṣasa even though his body is concealed by magic fall into the path of your sight at night and meet its destruction.
When the lord of men had spoken thus, he laughed and said to her: Līlā 1166. Thus addressed by the king, he laughed and spoke to her.
"Lord, this is the very last night of his life.
Having spoken thus, the king, his face and eyes filled with tears, grasped the mantra and summoned that female messenger of the night. (Līlā 1167–1168)
Then, O Kṛśodarī, having been granted many boons by that excellent sage, the king was sent away and went to his own abode at the end of the day. (Līlā.
1169) Meanwhile...

Then, having loosened the bond of its trunk, the elephant falls from the trees of the sky into the salt ocean— visible in the distance like a ripe, mango-colored drop of saffron on a dense dark cloud— as it abandons the river that serves as its vehicle. (Līlā 1170) Then.
When the moon had set, when the sun was obscured by the mass of darkness,
and when the multitude of people had settled into a peaceful sleep at midnight— then that lord of the night-dwellers, bearing himself with the arrogant pride of his own strength, [acted]. (Līlā 1171)
Two messengers, destroyers of enemies, were dispatched by the lord of men. They said:
"O King, listen; we have not been sent as mere messengers. Hear in full detail the matter that has been communicated to you by him. (Līlā 1172–1173)
"Just as these two watches of the final night are for my enjoyment,
whatever wealth dwells here shall become my food. (Līlā 1174) Therefore, O King, give me a hundred elephants at your own discretion.
"If you desire peace, offer me a great tribute of a thousand men, horses, and elephants.
(Līlā 1175) Having heard this, those messengers were addressed angrily by the lord of the earth:
"Go! You yourselves shall be the counter-messengers to that master of yours. (Līlā 1176)
"O you demon! Come here, so that I may give you an offering of flesh from my own waist, for the sake of the jackals and the howling dogs dwelling there! (Līlā 1177).
Having thus rebuked him in many other ways as well, the lord of the earth—
Both messengers, their anger having been provoked, were sent back.
(Līlā 1178) Then, after those night-stalkers had departed, the King commanded Kaṭāpāla:
"At dawn, let no one move from the fort. (Līlā 1179)
"With a single thousand of us, we can recall ten thousand heroic princesses; it is heard that the strength of those night-stalkers is likewise [great].
Having spoken thus, the king was surrounded there by a thousand heroes.
Having gone a great distance from his own village toward the night-stalkers, [he saw]— Līlā 1181—
[a place] difficult to behold due to the mass of fire emerging from mouths wide open and gaping,
and the sky made tawny by the sparks of the fire from the flickering swords of the Lallakkas. Līlā 1182.
The interior of the quarters was filled with the echoes of loud, far-reaching cries of "Phāra!
Phēkkāra!", while the forms of the throngs of people were revealed as the darkness was dispelled by the moonlight from her eyes.
Her mass of thick, coarse, and tawny hair was bound together with a fresh lotus stalk. (Līlā 11.83)
With their broad hips adorned with girdles made of garlands of human heads;
possessing the hue of bees, dark clouds, Tamāla trees, black collyrium, and the throat of a peacock;
that army of night-stalkers advanced toward the foremost of men. (Līlā 1184–1185)
The fierce nocturnal battle between the best of men and the rākṣasas proceeded with the sounds of *lalla*, *khakka*, *phēkkāra*, *mukka*, *ṇīsaṅka*, *kōkki*, and *bhaḍōha*. (Līlā.
1186) By some enraged night-stalker, a certain king was struck in such a manner.
Just as one whose body was emaciated by longing fell upon his fallen foe— Līlā 1187—
a certain great warrior, his neck severed by the stroke of a harsh sword,
brandished his circular blade even toward the fire of his own wrath— Līlā 1188.
A certain warrior, seized by the pride born of his own flesh-and-blood strength accumulated through the cessation of fainting, and whose enemy-force remains unsubdued, is dragged away by shame.
(Līlā 1189) For someone who has been struck down, the night becomes as if set ablaze by the fire of his wrath.
He drinks from her chest and hips, which are emitting the sound of belching and hissing.
(Līlā 1190) Even a warrior, though he has abandoned all hope for life, is avoided from afar by the moon out of fear, as if it were gripped in a firm fist. (Līlā 1191)
Seeing his army being struck down by those lords of faults whose bodies were concealed by illusion, the lord of the earth remembered that mantra;
for as soon as it was seen, it [the enemy] was struck by a blow from the sword. (Līlā. 1192)
The night-stalker was instantly struck down by the king who had become enraged.
Although he possessed incomparable strength, that terrifying-faced one was rendered breathless in an instant by the king, like a mountain struck by a wielder of the thunderbolt. (Līlāvatī 1193–1194)
Where throngs of piśācas shriek amidst heaps of severed heads, arms, and trunks;
where vetalas sink into the mire of flowing streams of fresh blood; and where hosts of Śiva’s attendants rejoice as they are surrounded by circles of approaching groups of dākinīs. (Līlā 11.95)

O beautiful one, in such a host of pure warriors—where packs of jackals howl as they gather around the circles of predatory scavengers; where the army of Rākṣasas is fleeing, feverish with the heat of battle; and where the entire multitude is thus [engaged]—[Līlā 1196–1197].
Filled with indignation born from seeing his own strength destroyed, that Rākṣasa, sword in hand like the moon, challenged the lord of men.
O Lord of Men, today is this very moment for you to experience the arrival of celestial women. (Līlā 1198)
"The day of the fear of imminent death has arrived; now is the hour.
(Līlā 1199) And the King said: "O Lord of Night-Rangers, at this hour the host of warriors emerges, each one close to the edge of another's sword.
(Līlā 1200)
"Bring them! If there is anyone like you who, when such a situation has arisen, can protect life for even a mere moment, even from the best of gods.
(Līlā 1201) While the lord of men was speaking thus, Bhīmānanā struck him with a blow.
O fawn-eyed one, out of anger he recited a *dohā* verse concerning Camarakaṇa.
(Līlā 1202) Even by the King, he—his neck-bond severed by the blow of a harsh sword—was suddenly cast down upon the earth, screaming most piteously. (Līlā 1203)

Then, by means of that [magical power], a man was produced who was of no other form than Pajjunna, possessing a splendor spreading forth like the extraordinary orb of the full moon at that very moment. Then, with cries of "Bravo! repeated again and again, that king [honored him]. *Līlāvaī* 1204. Then, by him, that lord of men [was honored] with the syllables of acclamation repeatedly.
Having greeted him, he said: "There is no one dearer to us than you. Therefore, O King, how much more need be said? This [Līlā] is yours;
whatever you desire, even if it be difficult to obtain, I shall give it to you, for it is already in my possession. (Līlā 1205–1206)
Having heard that, with a heart full of grace and curiosity arising within him, the King spoke:
"What indeed cannot be obtained from you? Therefore, let it be explained: who are you here, even though you are such as these? (Līlā 1207)
Līlā lived in the midst of those jackal-demons who subsist on raw flesh.
And he said: "O King, this must indeed be told by you in detail; for I have been ruined by my wicked addiction to killing demons. (Līlā 1208–1209)
Nevertheless, listen: there on this earth, the son of a Gandharva named Hema, whose heart is solely set upon bathing in the celestial river, has descended from heaven.
(Līlā 1210) Therefore, in that forest region, beautiful with trees at the foot of the snowy mountain, by me—
Truly, she is the peerless beauty of the three worlds, a gatherer of flowers.
(Līlā 1211) Then, approaching her side with curiosity and longing, I suddenly asked: "O gentle one, who are you? (Līlā 1212)
O Lord of Men, having heard that, she spoke these words to me with affection:
"I am here, indeed, the daughter of a forest-dwelling sage.
And I said, "O beautiful one, meeting us is not forbidden; therefore, now—" (Līlā 1213) [she continued].
I too have been born into a vast family of Gandharvas, named Cittaṅgada. Out of a longing to see you, I have descended here;
if you are well-disposed toward me, then that which was done by Love is appropriate. (Līlā 1214–1215)

Having spoken thus, O King, I married her there in the lonely forest according to my own rite—the daughter of an exceedingly great sage. Then, while she was experiencing that bliss comparable to the consecration of sovereignty over the three worlds... (Līlā 1216) ...I remained there.
O Lord of Men, he remained there until that sage also arrived.
And he said: "Kusumāla, you can endure our insult;
yet you are intoxicated by such a mere degree of wealth. (Līlā 1217–1218)
"Among those night-stalkers who contemplate sin, you shall become a flesh-eating demon for twelve years; such are you.
(Līlā 1219) Thus, when the twelve-year period had elapsed, [he was released] from the hands of the lords of men.
"You shall receive the severing of your head; then you will be released from this sorrow.
(Līlā 1220) "Therefore, this is the moment; now that you have been seen, what has happened has come to pass.
Tell us, my lady, what must we do? (Līlā 1221)
Having heard that, the king, his face suddenly blossoming with joy, said:
"Oh, we have been led far indeed by the mature wisdom of the good poet!
There is nothing further to be said than this which I am about to say. (Līlā 1222)
"Let that Kuvalayāvalī, her limbs emaciated by separation, be seen now!
(Līlā 1223) And he, his entire body suddenly bristling with intense horripilation, said:
"O King, even that which was spoken in jest produces supreme joy. (Līlā 1224)
"Without merit, such a thing as this could never happen to anyone;
nevertheless, I ask you: tell me now clearly the truth.
(Līlā 1225) Then, by him [the King], who possessed the beauty of a blue lotus petal, [she was addressed] as the son of the king of the Gandharvas...
The king spoke everything without remainder with joyful tears.
Then, with his eyes and face blossoming with the joy of a heart bowed in salutation, he said:
"Why does the son of Malayanila still remain? (Līlā 1226–1227)
At this juncture, Vijayānanda, his body filled with joy at the sight of Kuvalayadala’s beauty,
quickly went to Līlāvatī’s side.
Then Mādhavānila also arrived there, just as he had been thought of.
Accompanied by a thousand hosts of Siddhas, he arrived from the Malaya mountains.
That delight of the Gandharvas was welcomed by the daughter of the Siddha king;
like a rain of nectar, he showered her heart, and she him, as they gazed at one another. (Līlā 1229–1230)
Having agreed, they spoke with their limbs bristling with mutual joy;
having offered salutations to the gods, they congratulated themselves for a long time and held themselves in high esteem.
(Līlā 1231) At such a moment, Vijayānanda too, his eyes and face blossoming with delight—

Having had the princesses announced, he suddenly arrived at once. (Līlā 1232) Then, having offered a prostration from afar, he sat down before all three of them—Hāla and the others—upon a seat provided by the entire assembly. (Līlā 1233)
And the King said: "Dear kinsman, have you seen Mahānumati?
You clearly saw Kuvalayāvalī, her limbs wasted by the pangs of separation.
And he replied: "O King, we were seen sitting together on a single seat."
"It is known, it is known that the glories of the three worlds are [like] the three twilights.
(Līlā 1235) Having been informed and greeted, the Lord of Men arrived together with Citraṅgada, Mādhava, and Anila;
your heart's desire has been fulfilled. (Līlā 1236)
“O Blessed One, these very fruits, which have increased through long-term cultivation, are now being enjoyed by young people as the essence of the world.
Hearing this from them, [the king] was instantly covered in horripilation.
Each one, desiring to reveal their own face, held themselves in high esteem.

(Līlā 1238) Even when the meeting of all of them occurred—just as desired by their hearts—the Gandharvas, the lords of men, and the Siddhas did not believe it was real, even though it had come to pass. (Līlā 1239)
Even other women from the surrounding areas, eager to see the repetition [of the spectacle], ran immediately toward the palace;
for those whose minds were intent on proceeding toward the palace, even the path itself was not enough. (Līlā 12.40)
[He spoke] to the elders and to Nalakūvara, whose face was filled with joy.
Then Nalakūvara, together with his beloved and accompanied by his entire retinue, arrived right there at the same time as the swan-like lord of the Vidyādharas.
Then, having been congratulated by both the lord of the Vidyādharas and the lord of the Yakṣas, O King, each bestowed upon me a supreme jewel.
And it was said: "Report this repeatedly to Śālāhana. (Līlā. 1243)
"It is said: 'There is no other dear kinsman for us than you.
Therefore, let Mādhavānila be sent today with Citraṅgada;
the Yakṣas' wedding has been declared by the gods to take place without delay. (Līlā 1244–1245)
"Since it was said by Līlāvatī that the marriage of the kings would take place on another auspicious day, yet for you it has arrived at this very moment.
Having heard that, the lord of men [spoke] to her whose eyes were like the full moon or the young deer.
From Vijayānanda, Siddhādhivinandana was addressed:
"O Lord, we have heard what was sent by Nalakūvara through his messenger;
go now with Cittaṅgaya to that place which is desired by our hearts. (Līlā 1247–1248)
Accompanied by the fourfold great musical instruments, by auspicious sounds from various drums,
and by the resonance of conchs, trumpets, and muiṅgas, they set forth, preceded by the joy of victory and celebrated by lovely songs. (Līlā 1249)
Accompanied by pairs of friends residing in that region,
the two of them approached, having performed the salutation at the feet of Nalakūvara as he arrived before them,
longing for the sight of him as he came to meet their father.

They saw each other’s beloveds; and by both of them, with pairs of eyes fixed upon one another's face, their beloveds were gazed upon repeatedly. (Līlā 1252) Then, with hearts hanging over the precipice of separation, they failed to attain the enjoyment of happiness.
What were our beloveds not made to say by means of humble entreaties? O dear ones, show us favor! What can we say?
Cast into the mire of a grave offense, we have been scorched by that [fate] for so long through the power of ill fortune.
Thus having been thus informed by Mādhavānila,
that daughter of the Yakṣa king was taken there hand-to-hand by him, O fawn-eyed one.
(Līlā 1255) Then she [was bathed] with water from the tips of his fingernails, which were trembling and dripping with perspiration.

A lover gives the price of a dear reunion even for the mere touch of a hand; thus, his body filled with horripilation from the thrill of the touch of his beloved’s hand, Mādhavānila ascended the palace roof with great joy. (Līlā 1256–1257)

With his eyes alone, he—his mind overflowing with affection—as if embraced, kissed, dallied with, and drank her in; even though she was but a painting on the couch adorned with strings of jewels before him. (Līlā 1258)
Seated there, his eyes fixed upon the lotus-face of his beloved, [Lavaṅgika says:
"At this very moment, O one with the beauty of a blue-lotus petal, a messenger has been swiftly dispatched by Līlāvatī to her own family home in a boat.
When the moon had risen and the auspicious hour for the wedding ceremony had been completed,
the Yakṣa ladies prepared the pavilion grounds, their vast perimeters strewn with sprouts that seemed to rival the beauty of the gods' own celestial trees. (Līlā 12.61)
The earth was fashioned, yellowish-red with the offering of excellent flowers.
Then, surrounded by her own beloved friends and attendants, having attained supreme joy, she sat upon various charming grounds that had been repeatedly cleared away. (Līlā 1262–1263)
Various drinks, bright with various colors,
scented with the fragrance of sahakāra flowers and perfumed with the aroma of blue lotuses, are being served—
drinks whose mouths are made resonant by bees clustering around the scent of the wine, as soon as they are seen. (Līlā 1264)

In the houses of wanton women, the gaze becomes languid with passion. (Līlā 1265) Right at the outset, by the power increased through long-standing addiction to wine, the god of love has his bow bent by the hand resting upon the goblet. (Līlā 1266)
The more wine is drunk, the more slowly one's intoxication fades;
the more the intoxication subsides, the more her beauty ascends.
(Līlā 1267) What has been spoken long ago is remembered, but even what was said just a moment ago is quickly forgotten.

Even an improper thing spoken charms when accompanied by the intoxication of honey-wine. (Līlā 1268) A certain woman, whose face was turned upward with suppressed indignation, is later appeased by her lover, even though she had been embraced for the offense committed while she was unconscious from the excess of honey-wine. (Līlā 1269)
Even when she has been kissed by her beloved, who has pressed his honey-red cheeks against hers, she removes the sprout-like tears from her ears;
there, the lover drinks [her tears], which touch upon her transgression and uproot her tree of pride.
(Līlā 1270) The beloved drinks [the tears] that touch upon her offense and uproot the tree of her jealous anger.
The wine, poured from mouths held by the hands of their lovers,

is drunk with difficulty after a long time by pairs of Siddhas who had been sleeping happily in the pleasure of drinking the nectar of each other’s lips, now their faces betraying signs of embarrassment. (Līlā 12.71–72)
Some beloved, after a long time, drinks the autumn wine— which has been warmed by the breath of her lover’s face—
little by little as if it were nectar, having tasted it from her rival who was full of anger.
(Līlā 1273) [She performs] a song with hand-clapping, a dance with the face as a maddala drum, and laughter.
She endures the faces of the wanton women, brightened by their radiant smiles.

(Līlā 1274) The women of pleasure endure [the sight of him] as their waistbands slip slightly, their girdles fall away, their veils drop, their forehead-ornaments are slightly disarranged, and they are somewhat intoxicated. (Līlā 1275)

Then, at the time of the conclusion of the third day, while the multitude of Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and other beings were still intoxicated with the remnants of their honey-wine, Śilāmegha arrived together with his beloved, as all of them had gathered in one place. (Līlā 1276) Then he [met] his beloved, along with everyone who had assembled in that single spot.
He sat down instantly before the leaders of the *vidyādharas* and others.
Having observed him, O beautiful one, that mountain was addressed by all of them after they had experienced the pleasure of seeing their beloved daughter: (Līlā 1277–1278).
Having arrived at the excellent palace of his beloved daughter along with the splendor of the lake,
he beheld that Līlāvatī, whose eyes were like the petals of the blue water-lily.
Having smelled the crown of her head, she rose from her prostration and drew near.
Held in her mother’s lap, with a silver ornament upon her and her body moist with affection— Līlā.1280—
she was released by her father while she was observing the words of the Vidyādharas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and humans. Līlā.1281.
At that moment, while she was delighted by the reunion with her kinsmen,
she remembered even that period of her pregnancy which had been described by Gaṇeśa.
Then, having been recognized in due course by her elders and relatives, she sat down.

The celebration was proclaimed with special distinction by everyone. (Līlā 1283) Then, the festivities were joyous and hurried with delight, accompanied by the sounds of auspicious cries uttered by those satisfied by a succession of joys, while the attendants danced with great splendor.
(Līlā 1284)
On another day, at the beginning of the day when all his forces were pre-eminent,
Kuvalayāvalī took her bath and arrived before the king.
Then he [saw her] standing in the center of the courtyard fashioned in the middle of the glorious pavilion.
With a beautiful surrounding halo of golden pitchers placed at its four corners;
with its vast expanse strewn with the splendor of fresh *haḍa* and *pāuāra* gems;
and with a wide extent covered by a canopy of diamonds, sapphires, and emeralds. (Līlā 1286–1287)
Seated upon the pleasure-pavilion, which was filled with the increasing splendor and wealth made manifest by the kindled golden lamps,
the lord of men enjoyed complete happiness,
being praised by the Gandharva nymphs and sung to by the throngs of Siddhas. (Līlā 1288)
First, he was bathed by the playful Vidyādharīs and Yakṣīs;
then, amidst the great sounds of various auspicious musical instruments,
he was bathed there by Rambhā, who was overflowing with laughter.
Mounted upon an elephant with tusks like ivory, adorned with white garments and white flowers, anointed with white sandalwood paste, and bearing a white lotus, he set forth. (Līlā.
1291) He was accompanied by the lords of the Vidyādharas, headed by Nala and Kūvara, who had come forward to meet him.
"I have been seen by all of you this very half-day with my head bowed in salutation"— so [he spoke].
Then, preceded by those very same [companions], the lord of men reached the residence of the King of Siṃhala, O lady with eyes like the full moon.
That [place] which was adorned with various painted figures of birds and beasts arranged in rows of colors,
where the rainbow of the gods was eclipsed by the mass of rays from beautiful ornaments,
and whose charming ground was strewn with many kinds of variegated flowers— Līlā 1294.
The entrance to the pavilion was adorned with pearl necklaces hanging down to the level of the divine fingers;
it resounded with auspicious music blended with the beating of drums, conchs, and kāhala trumpets, and was heart-stealing with the playful jests of the assembly of young women. (Līlā 1295–1296)
That auspicious vessel of curd, honey, and ghee, containing the sacrificial offering for the king, was placed upon the golden surface;
meanwhile, the lord of men, having opened the door out of curiosity for his beloved, waited there. (Līlā 1297)
After a long time, having arrived and sat down upon a cushion of cotton-wool,
King Līlāvaī was beheld by the king with joyful emotion— she whose lotus-face was adorned with a sparse arrangement of jasmine flowers. (Līlā 1298–1299)

Being gratified and delighted by the young women with playful jests, the lord of men remained there for a long time; then, having ascended his palanquin, he was carried by four porters and, having attained supreme joy, [proceeded]. (Līlā 1300)
Having offered prostrations to the Guru, he sat down once again there.
(Līlā 1301) Then, as the King was descending from his palanquin, a certain woman from Siṅghalaṅgaṇa, seated upon a couch on the terrace of the Āratti palace, approached before him.
(Līlā 1302)
Then, by that bard of the Vidyādharas, with his face suddenly blossoming, a collection of verses (*gāthā*)—both adorned and most charming—was recited: "O King, behold!
Seated upon the lotuses that are her feet, with anklets like pairs of *kalahaṃsa* swans, she—motionless as she rests close to one another, with peaceful sounds of conversation—is as if sleeping;
her broad thighs are joined within by a sword-blade that has been drawn forth from its scabbard. (Līlā 1304)
As if transferred to the petals of her tongue, the glance delights in the lover.

(Līlā 1305) Upon her belly, which is slender and surrounded by waves of three folds that are slightly uneven and not too wide apart, the line of body hair shines even more brightly, appearing as if it were fixed there permanently. (Līlā 1306)
The light of the lamp, its halo produced by the beauty overflowing from the pair of arms extended in longing, spreads far and wide, though it has found no firm footing;
it is being gathered in by the uneven flickering as it brushes against her swaying, trembling thighs. (Līlā 1307)
The necklace, distressed by the separation from the circle of her neck, wanders about.
(Līlā 1308) Adorned upon her breast, the necklace, with its gems flashing like flickering lamps, appears like the flowing Ganges descending from the peak of Mount Meru. (Līlā 1308A)
With the expanse of her lashes thickened by the luster of her broad, polished collyrium,
her youthful gaze wanders like a young peacock’s tail-feather together with its train. O King, thus for a thousand years has this [gaze] of yours been unobserved by old age.

Let the lamp of the festival be carried about out of curiosity. (Līlā 1310) Then, at the onset of night, that lord of men, the king, eager for the pleasure of dalliance, entered his bedchamber together with his beloved. (Līlā 1311)
"O you whose face is like the *kuvalaya* lotus, what is the use of much speaking now? That night has passed while that king remained awake.
Thus, when dawn had arrived, all those divine beings [spoke].
Having honored him greatly, the Yakṣa, the lord of the Siddhas, bestowed upon the king his own various supernatural powers:
the power of invisibility, an inexhaustible treasury, and the ability to travel through the sky by means of the Gandharva art. (Līlāvatī 1313–1314)
The swan also gave him the medicinal elixir of vermilion, accepted the mantra, and whatever else there was, that too was at your disposal.
Having thus agreed in many ways, O gentle lady, he departed toward his own city. (Līlā 1315)
The king, filled with joy and agitation, departed together with Līlāvatī. (Līlā.
1316) In the meantime, those Vidyādharas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, and Gandharvas also arrived suddenly and with great delight at their own respective abodes. (Līlā. 1319A)
Likewise, that Śilāmegha also, having gone two *prasthas* and then turned back, gave his jeweled ornaments to Tanayā;
accompanied by the beauty of autumn and surrounded by his servants, he went to Siṃhaladvīpa. (Līlā 13.20)
His joy increased by the happiness of the completed marriage with Līlāvatī. Līlā 1320A.
Then, O gentle one, that king, having attained the fulfillment born of winning Līlāvatī, returned to his own place with ever-increasing auspiciousness. Līlā 1320B.
"O Best of Men, may these days pass unnoticed for you, spent in the company of this Līlāvatī, who is unaging for a thousand years; let the days go by unseen. (Līlā.
1317) Having thus offered blessings in various ways to the lord of men, the hosts of yakṣas—

They all arrived there immediately, each hastening toward their own respective dwellings. (Līlā 1318) Having performed worship to the Three-eyed Lord with devotion and having gracefully bowed to the naked ascetic, the lotus-eyed Śālāhana departed. (Līlā 1319)
Likewise, Śilāmegha also returned after traveling two *prasthas*, having given his jeweled ornaments to Tanaā.
King Pṛthvīśvara, his eyes directed by the words of Lolāvati, was filled with satisfaction. (Līlā 13.20)

Gladdened by the bliss of knowledge, he proceeds with supreme grace. (Līlā 1321) His elephants, terrifying the enemy with the fear inspired by the presence of his great feudatories, quickly reached the capital, the seat of sovereign power. (Līlā 1322)

That city, which was beautiful with the splendor of lofty arches and high towers, crowded with shining temples and gardens, and possessed lofty ramparts; its ramparts were delighted by the gardens that possessed the charm of jewels as firm as diamonds. (Līlā 13.23)
[The moon] reflected in the nearby streams scattered by the wind,
[and] rising high upon the breasts of beautiful women— which were like rising clouds and which shone with a gentle pressure from the reflection— terrifying the travelers. (Līlā 13.24–25)

In the midst of this [city], where the paths are called out by the clamor of travelers' cries, where the crowds of good people have their eyes fixed upon the various and wonderful treasures deposited in the treasury, and which is adorned with golden pillars and jewels— Līlā 1326. In its center, there is a golden pillar shimmering with jewels.
The king arrived at the great palace of the queen in that very moment.
Having paid homage and remained with his feet touching hers— she by whom all stains of sin and impurity had been washed away—
the king truly went to his own residence amidst a shower of colored powders.
Here concludes this narrative theme, expanded from its concise form; having been told with great detail, who indeed would be able to conceive of it? (Līlā 1329).
And it was said by the beloved, composed in the Marāṭha regional dialect.
The limbs of this story are worthy of association with the virtuous.
(Līlā 1330) Whatever has been accepted by the heart of our beloved here is not to be grasped by the wise as it appears on the surface, but rather according to its true intent. (Līlā 1331)
Enough with those who judge merits and faults based solely on their own likes and dislikes; for what do they know of the true essence of poetry?

Only those of middle capacity, who are impartial regarding merit and fault, understand the ultimate meaning of literary works. This [work] has been composed in a measure of eighteen thousand verses, excluding the introductory stanzas.
"This is now concluded; how [could it be otherwise] regarding the one named Līlāvatī?
(Līlā 1333) "O long-eyed one, for those who read or hear this story every day, there shall never be the pain of separation from their beloved, O slender-limbed one. (Līlā 1333A)
Thus ends the narrative titled *Līlāvatī*.
